articles.title: Hierarchical knowledge and skills undermine payoff-biased social learning
articles.authors: Nanda Ramo Jafarian; Björn Lindström; Ingmar Visser; Annemie Ploeger; Pieter van den Berg; Lucas Molleman
articles.abstract: Acquiring skills and knowledge (“traits”) through social learning is central to human development and cultural evolution. Yet it remains unclear how individuals can effectively learn from others when traits form hierarchies, with advanced traits building on more basic ones. We present a model showing that trait hierarchies favour “proximal social learning” where individuals copy others who are only slightly more knowledgeable. In contrast, payoff bias - often assumed to be universally advantageous - performs poorly because it directs learners toward advanced traits they lack the basics for. Our experiments demonstrate that people indeed shift to proximal social learning when conditions favour it. Our results challenge core assumptions of mainstream cultural evolution theory and highlight that trait hierarchies are a key factor shaping human social learning.

articles.title: From Knowing to Doing: ADHD and the Enactment of Chronic Pain Self-Management in Youth—A Conceptual Review
articles.authors: Mahdieh Vaezbarenji; David Moore; Edmund Sonuga-Barke
articles.abstract: Young people with chronic pain are routinely asked to carry out multicomponent self-management plans with limited day-to-day support. ADHD traits are common, and often unrecognised, among young people attending paediatric pain services, yet little is known about how an ADHD profile shapes the way they act on these plans. This conceptual review argues that some apparent non-adherence in this group reflects a knowing-to-doing gap: a mismatch between the demands of treatment plans and the executive and motivational profile associated with ADHD, rather than a lack of knowledge or concern. Drawing on ADHD, prospective memory, paediatric chronic illness, and health-behaviour research, we identify where this mismatch is most likely to occur: remembering to act at the right time, starting without a prompt, monitoring progress, and resuming after interruption. As direct evidence is lacking, we set out testable propositions: executive differences predict enactment beyond knowledge and intention; the gap widens when plans require independent organisation and narrows with external structure; and inconsistent enactment contributes to later pain-related disability. Clinically, services should identify where enactment breaks down before attributing it to low effort, and adapt plans through simpler actions, routines, prompts, and coordinated home–school–clinic support.

articles.title: Actual use of generative AI chatbots for mental health advice across adulthood: Psychological correlates and the moderating role of age
articles.authors: Angeliki Triantafillaki; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Panagiota Peleka; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: Little is known about which adults actually turn to generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice, and whether the profile of these users changes with age. The aim of this study was to examine the sociodemographic and psychological correlates of actual chatbot consultation for mental health advice, and of its frequency. In this cross-sectional online survey, 843 Greek adults aged 18 to 50 years reported whether, and how often, they had consulted an AI chatbot about their thoughts and feelings during the previous three months. Validated instruments captured anxiety, depression, loneliness, sleep quality, self-esteem and problematic social media use. Logistic and proportional odds models, extended with age-by-predictor product terms, were fitted. Seven in ten respondents (71.3%) reported such use, and 37.5% did so weekly or more often. Independent correlates of any use were younger age, recent consultation with a mental health professional, greater problematic social media use and lower self-esteem. Among users, worse sleep, lower self-esteem and greater problematic social media use were associated with more frequent consultation of AI chatbots for mental health advice. Age moderated the role of loneliness, which was related to chatbot use only among the youngest respondents, and a comparable but weaker gradient emerged for depressive symptoms. Chatbot-based mental health advice is now widespread among Greek adults up to midlife. Clinicians should ask patients of every age about it, and preventive efforts should recognize that its psychological drivers are not uniform across adulthood.

articles.title: Gender and Agency in AI Career Guidance for Women: A Socio-Technical Audit of General-Purpose Language Models
articles.authors: Sara Portell Fonolla; Yasmina El Fassi
articles.abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. Studies of gender bias in large language model (LLM) career advice mostly score single outputs about a person described to the model. But career guidance is a conversation with the woman herself, in which the advice can end up making the decision for her or treat a barrier she faces as a lack of confidence. We report a preregistered socio-technical audit of the career guidance that ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give women through their APIs. We scripted 34 multi-turn conversations grounded in research on women’s careers, ran each five times per system, and added male versions of 14 to test gender cues (972 conversations). Human raters scored 304 conversations on nine objectives drawn from that research and from coaching ethics, with a second rater and an expert adjudicator for disagreements. Failures to preserve her agency had the highest share for every system (36% to 50% of conversations scored 1 or above on a 0 to 3 scale) and were more frequent than gender bias failures. Gemini was more often sycophantic. Swapping the user's gender showed no systematic difference, but pair differences depended on how the name was given. No LLM judge agreed acceptably with human raters, and the human raters also often disagreed, so the rates are descriptive. Audits of AI career advice should use more than one gender cue and, because models change, be repeated over time. LLM judges can serve as a screening aid, but scoring needs two or more human experts.

articles.title: Theoretical Challenges in Psychology in the 2000s: Top-5
articles.authors: Vladislav Medintsev
articles.abstract: Psychology entered the twenty-first century with an exceptionally large empirical base and a conspicuously thin theoretical infrastructure. The expansion of cognitive neuroscience, the institutionalization of evidence-based practice, and mounting evidence of a replication crisis exposed foundational assumptions to scrutiny of a kind the discipline had not faced since the paradigm debates of the mid-twentieth century. This article offers a structured critical overview of the five most consequential theoretical problems that shaped psychological science between 2000 and 2010 and traces their trajectory through 2026. The problems are ranked according to three explicit criteria—logical priority, breadth of disciplinary impact, and urgency for scientific and applied practice—and the ranking itself is defended as an argument, with alternative orderings considered and rejected. The resulting order is: (1) fragmentation of psychological theory and the absence of a unifying metatheory; (2) the crisis of construct validity and operationalism; (3) the mind–brain identity problem and the reductionism debate; (4) the cultural challenge to universalist assumptions; and (5) the methodological–epistemological tension between positivist and interpretivist traditions. Each problem is analyzed with respect to its antecedents, its specific manifestations during the 2000s, and the partial responses advanced in the subsequent decade and a half. The central claim is that the five problems form an interlocking system whose keystone is metatheoretical fragmentation; because the terms in which the remaining four problems are stated presuppose unsettled metatheoretical commitments, piecemeal reform cannot produce durable resolution. The concluding section outlines a research agenda centered on integrative theoretical reconstruction and epistemologically grounded methodological pluralism.

articles.title: Inward-directed utterances and the evolution of language
articles.authors: Conor Houghton
articles.abstract: At some point in our evolutionary history humans gained the ability to communicate using language. Most accounts of language evolution focus on its role in communication. This review proposes an alternative: that the decisive step was the internalisation of utterance as a tool for directing thought. A hierarchy of animal communication is developed to sharpen this proposal. Evidence from the development of language in children supports the view that internalisation is central to language acquisition. The success of chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models provides a further, independent demonstration of the importance of language as a tool. These proposals together suggest that language is patterned on the structure of thought rather than shaped primarily by the demands of communication.

articles.title: The Morality of Partiality: How Relationship Expectations Shape Moral Evaluations
articles.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Amiya Shelly Aggarwal; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Alexander C. Walker
articles.abstract: While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations. The present research (N = 2,353) examined how people evaluate partial and impartial actors who prioritized either a socially connected other (family member, friend, or community member) or a stranger in need. Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors. This preference was strongest when impartial actors failed to prioritize a close (family member or friend), rather than more distant (community member), social tie. Impartial actors were also perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their relational obligations, with these perceptions predicting judgments of their moral character. In Experiment 4, participants themselves exhibited a preference for partiality, with most preferring to help a socially connected other over a stranger in greater need. This preference was stronger when decisions were described as publicly observable rather than anonymous, consistent with reputational concerns influencing helping decisions. Together, these findings suggest that everyday moral judgments reflect not only assessments of adherence to abstract ethical principles but also inferences about individuals’ reliability as long-term social partners.

articles.title: Social media addiction is associated with poor mental health, AI chatbot use, and problematic digital behaviours among Generation Z: a cross-sectional study in Greece
articles.authors: Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Angeliki Triantafillaki; Panagiota Peleka; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Olga Galani; Maria Tsiachri; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE To examine the association between social media addiction and mental health among members of Generation Z in Greece. Moreover, we examined the association between social media addiction and social media-related behaviours. METHOD We conducted a web-based cross-sectional study with a convenience sample of 599 individuals aged 18 to 29 years. We measured social media addiction with the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Outcomes were anxiety, depression, loneliness, social media fatigue, sleep quality, life satisfaction, physician visits for mental health issues, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot use for mental health issues, second-screen use, social media distraction, fear of missing out, and no-social-media phobia. We performed multivariable logistic regression analysis adjusting for sex, age, and financial status, and we examined interactions between social media addiction and these variables. RESULTS Overall, 56.6% of participants were addicted to social media. The prevalence of anxiety was 57.5% among addicted participants and 38.1% among non-addicted participants, while the prevalence of depression was 39.2% and 25.8%, respectively. After adjustment for confounders, social media addiction was associated with higher odds of anxiety, depression, loneliness, social media fatigue, poor sleep quality, life dissatisfaction, and AI chatbot use for mental health issues. Also, social media addiction was associated with higher odds of second-screen use, social media distraction, fear of missing out, and no-social-media phobia. Sex, age, and financial status did not substantially modify these associations. CONCLUSIONS Social media addiction is highly prevalent among Generation Z and is associated with several mental health problems and problematic digital behaviours. Interventions to prevent social media addiction and to facilitate access to professional mental health care among young people are needed.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of Tai Chi exercise on psychological distress in older adults: A reassessment of Xu and Yang (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Xu and Yang concluded an association between Tai Chi exercise and reduced psychological distress among older adults, and that this association was mediated by reduced negative mood state and increased sleep quality. However, mediated effects, like correlations in general, in observational data may be spurious, e.g., due to confounding by a shared cause of the variables. Here, a reassessment indicated that direct, indirect (i.e., mediated), and total effects of Tai Chi exercise on psychological distress reported by Xu and Yang were indistinguishable from effects implied by a model where the measured variables were specified as indicators of a shared latent cause. Hence, the effects reported by Xu and Yang may have been spurious and their conclusions premature. Researchers are recommended to evaluate if mediated effects survive adjustment for a potential shared cause of the predictor, mediator(s), and outcome before making claims about genuine mediation.

articles.title: Prior Experience and the Production of Unfamiliar Linguistic Forms: Evidence from Sign Language
articles.authors: Monica Xiao Wei; Diar Abdlkarim; Sang-Hoon Yeo; Robin Thompson
articles.abstract: Producing unfamiliar linguistic forms requires learners to map perceived phonological structure onto articulatory actions. Sign languages provide a useful context for examining how prior language-specific and sensorimotor experience relate to this process. Three groups (N = 105) reproduced 96 Hong Kong Sign Language signs varying in phonological complexity: L1/early British Sign Language signers, hearing musicians, and hearing non-signing controls. Performance was assessed using phonological accuracy across five parameters and kinematic similarity to signing models using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). Mixed-effects analyses showed significant effects of group, complexity, and their interaction for both outcomes. Signers showed the highest phonological accuracy and greatest kinematic similarity. Musicians showed higher phonological accuracy than controls, whereas their overall kinematic similarity did not differ significantly. Higher phonological accuracy was moderately associated with greater kinematic similarity. These findings suggest that the relationship between prior experience and unfamiliar linguistic production varies according to both the type of experience and the aspect of production measured.

articles.title: Structural Equation Modeling with Word-Embedding for Text-Based Measurement
articles.authors: Artur Pokropek; Hubert Plisiecki; Maria Flakus; Adam Waszkowski; Kinga Małyska; Tomasz Żółtak
articles.abstract:
In recent years, advances in natural language processing have led researchers to increasingly use
text-based data to study various psychological and social phenomena. This usually goes without
an explicit measurement model or evaluation of the psychometric properties of text-based
indicators. We introduce SEM-WE, which fits measurement and structural models to correlation
matrices that are based on word embeddings derived from texts under study. Each construct is
represented by several indicator words or phrases. The centered cosine matrix provides the input
for estimating loadings, residuals, model fit statistics, reliability indicators, and parameters
describing relations between constructs. We use a synthetic corpus, a survey study that combines
both textual and Likert-type questions, and real-life posts from X in a multi-study validation
exercise. Using simulated persona attitudes, self-ratings, and human coding as benchmarks, we
compare six approaches: dictionary stance counts, embedding centroids based on positive
indicators alone, embedding centroids contrasting positive and negative indicators, annotations by
a local language model, annotations by a frontier language model, and SEM-WE. SEM-WE
reproduces benchmark signs in these examples and their ordering at least as well as other methods,
matching or outperforming most competitors under the reported configurations. Dictionary and
centroid results vary more across reported configurations, while large language models perform
well in the synthetic and survey studies; however, at much higher computational cost.

articles.title: When Objects Act Together: EEG Evidence for Enhanced Neural Reinstatement Following Action-Based Unitization
articles.authors: Véronique Huffer; Axel Mecklinger; Roni Tibon
articles.abstract: Unitization is the process of integrating items into one entity providing the possibility to subsequently remembering these associations via familiarity. According to cortical reinstatement accounts, successful retrieval depends on the degree to which encoding-related neural activity is reactivated when the memory is later accessed. The goal of the current study was to investigate whether action relationships as a bottom-up unitization approach alter the correspondence between neural representations formed during encoding and those reinstated during associative retrieval. Younger and older adults (N = 47) studied semantically unrelated object pairs that were either arranged in a way that an action could be imagined (unitized, e.g., a milk bottle above a shoe) or not (non-unitized, e.g., a shoe above a milk bottle). Afterwards, they had to distinguish between old, recombined and new object pairs. Encoding-Retrieval Similarity (ERS) was used to assess item-specific similarity of EEG-based neural activation at encoding and retrieval. Across both age groups, greater similarity was observed for same object pairs (i.e., item specific pairs) than for different object pairs. Critically, however, in the time window traditionally associated with familiarity (300-500ms post-stimulus), larger ERS was observed for action-related than action-unrelated object pairs, but only when same object pairs were presented at encoding and retrieval. These findings suggest that action relationships increase the reinstatement of pair-specific encoding representations, even though the direct functional link between this enhanced reinstatement and associative memory benefit remains open.

articles.title: Why faster thinkers are smarter thinkers: Working memory binding as the link between processing speed and cognitive ability
articles.authors: Anna-Lena Schubert; Linda Eileen Leydecker; Henrike Maria Jungeblut; Mareike Hülsemann
articles.abstract: Individuals who process information faster tend to score higher on cognitive ability tests, but the mechanism linking processing speed to general cognitive ability (g) remains unresolved. We tested whether this association is mediated by working memory capacity, and if so, whether the critical component is executive attention — as captured by complex span tasks requiring dual-task coordination and interference management — or relational binding — the ability to form and maintain temporary associations between unrelated features. In a community sample of 215 adults (aged 18–40), we measured processing speed at both the neural level (ERP component peak latencies) and the cognitive level (diffusion model drift rates), working memory through complex span and binding tasks, and g through a comprehensive cognitive ability test battery. Latent variable mediation analyses showed that complex span performance only partially mediated the speed–g relationship, leaving significant direct effects. In contrast, binding task performance fully mediated the relationship for cognitive processing speed and substantially mediated it for neural processing speed, reducing previously significant direct paths to nonsignificance. When both mediators competed in parallel models, binding emerged as the dominant predictor of g, with complex span contributing no unique variance. These findings identify relational binding as the specific working memory component that transmits the association between processing speed and cognitive ability, suggesting that the cognitive bottleneck linking processing speed to reasoning ability is not executive control but the more elemental ability to build and maintain temporary relational representations.

articles.title: Loneliness and the human brain: insights from neuroimaging and priorities for future research
articles.authors: Christian K. Tamnes; Livia Tomova
articles.abstract: Loneliness, the subjective experience of a perceived discrepancy between desired and actual social connection, is robustly associated with poor mental and physical health across the lifespan. Although not uniformly increasing in prevalence, loneliness is rising among adolescents and young adults, making it an important public health concern. Neuroimaging offers a means to examine the neural pathways through which loneliness emerges and affects health. A growing body of structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging research implicates differences in regions and networks central to social cognition, internally directed thought, episodic memory, and executive control, most consistently the default mode network, medial temporal structures, and prefrontal cortex. In this Perspective, we review this literature, critically assess its limitations, and outline priorities for future research, including the need for refined measurement, longitudinal developmental and experimental designs, and integration with genetic and contextual factors.

articles.title: Positive Affect is Associated with Interactive Social Media Use: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Evelyn Alice Halliday Murray; Daniel Shaw; Jisun Kim; Andrew Jones; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington
articles.abstract: Research examining associations between social media usage (SMU) and adolescent psychological wellbeing has relied on cross-sectional self-report data, limiting understanding of specific social media behaviours and within-person variability. To address these limitations, the present study combined an objective experimental task with Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) to investigate associations between adolescents’ SMU styles, momentary affect, and trait depressive symptoms. 229 older adolescents (110 females; Mage = 22.60, 18-25 years old) completed the Social Networking Site Behaviour Task, which classifies SMU along a passive to interactive continuum, across three days (573 datapoints). Trait depressive symptoms were assessed on Day 1 using the Maryland Trait and State Depression Scale, while momentary affect was measured on each day using the International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Linear mixed-effects models revealed between-person variability in SMU style. Positive affect was significantly associated with more interactive SMU (liking and commenting relative to scrolling), whereas negative affect and trait depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with SMU style. Our findings suggest that SMU styles reflect both stable individual differences and dynamic within-person variation associated with positive affective states. This demonstrates the value of combining objective behavioural measures with longitudinal EMA design to advance understanding SMU and psychological wellbeing.

articles.title: A Simple Introduction to the Effects of Measurement Error and Omitted Interactions in the Context of Linear Regression
articles.authors: Aljoscha Rimpler; Henk Kiers; Don van Ravenzwaaij
articles.abstract: Many technical texts exist on the potential problems of measurement error (i.e., variables are measured imperfectly) and the inclusion of interaction effects in linear regression. Such resources are typically rife with techniques that may or may not solve the situation (e.g, mean-centering) depending on the presence or absence of certain conditions (e.g., multicollinearity). Understanding such texts can be daunting to applied researchers, especially as visualizations of the potential effects of these are typically lacking. We provide a Shiny app to help users better understand and anticipate such situations. Based on user-specified input, the app allows users to compare a model that includes only linear effects to a model that additionally includes an interaction effect when such an interaction exists. It allows comparisons of the effects on regression weights, their bias and variance at different evaluation points, confidence regions for regression surfaces, model fit, and model differentiability. This information should ultimately help researchers to understand the problem at hand and align their substantive research objectives with their modeling choices better. Thus, the app is a useful tool towards both learning about and teaching about potential pitfalls of simple linear regression and is aimed at applied researchers in the social sciences.

articles.title: Children’s acquisition of cardinal number gestures: Evidence of knower levels and a relationship to number word acquisition
articles.authors: Allie Tung; Mikka Hoffman; Kara Weisman; Dominic Gibson
articles.abstract: While research on children’s number development largely focuses on number words (e.g., “two”) as an indicator of children’s knowledge, less is known about how children acquire knowledge of other number systems, such as cardinal number gestures (e.g., holding up two fingers to represent two objects). Examining children’s learning across multiple number systems can shed light on what aspects of number learning may be specific to a particular system or may reflect underlying conceptual development. In the current study, we tested 2.5- to 4-year-olds’ knowledge of number gestures and number words (n = 175) and found that children may learn number gestures through a series of knower level stages, similar to the well-established process of number word development. Following approaches used by studies with bilingual children, we found that children’s knowledge of number gestures predicted their knowledge of number words, statistically controlling for age and counting ability. We observed this relationship among both the full sample and among only subset-knowers (i.e., children who only understand a subset of the numbers that they can count to), suggesting that children’s number word and gesture development may be linked throughout the developmental process. These findings provide insight into the structure of children’s number gesture knowledge and how this knowledge may relate to their broader number development.

articles.title: Mapping the noetic quality: A computational analysis of the elicitors and experience of profound truth
articles.authors: Vi Bui; Paul Joseph Silvia
articles.abstract: Profound experiences have been studied under many constructs in psychology, such as mystical and religious experiences, aesthetic experiences, awe, and the sublime. Despite differing in appraisal structure, emotional content and valence, and typical triggers, common among their nomological networks seems to be the noetic quality: the subjective sense of apprehending something which feels nonrational but true, self-evident, immediate, and real. This suggests that the noetic quality might be a unique and separable phenomenon. It has rarely been studied as such, however, partly because these experiences tend to be highly subjectively intense and specific, making them difficult to induce in a laboratory and their retrospective accounts costly to analyze qualitatively. In the present study, we analyzed a sample of N = 318 participants who wrote narrative essays about their experiences with the noetic quality and answered questions about their emotional and motivational content, and subjective epistemic change. Essays were classified using natural language processing. Elicitors spanned aesthetic experiences, psychedelic experiences, religious and mystical experiences, and experiences with death, and experiences were affectively heterogeneous (34% negative, 66% positive). Across elicitors, experiences were consistently marked by high emotional intensity, action tendency, and subjective epistemic change, suggesting an emotion-like structure. The study demonstrates the feasibility of computational approaches for studying rare and non-ordinary experiences.

articles.title: Dispositifs of the Narrative: A New Poststructuralist Radicalization of Narrative Therapy
articles.authors: Cristopher Yáñez-Urbina
articles.abstract: Narrative therapy made narration the medium of its clinical work and the means through which it contests the truths of psychology; the status it grants the narrative shapes its accounts of knowledge, subject, problem, and change. This article reconstructs that status in White and Epston and in the poststructuralist radicalizations of Madigan and Guilfoyle. The tradition historicized psychopathological truths and the authority of expert knowledge and stabilized certain narrative properties (temporal sequence, biographical coherence, and attribution to a subject) as general conditions for understanding experience, an asymmetry of historicization. Taking Foucault's concept of dispositif as he formulated it, we shift the object of analysis from narratives to dispositifs of the narrative, configurations of discursive and nondiscursive practices, relations of force, and practices of the self within which narrating oneself becomes possible, required, and credible. Because the asymmetry concerns forms that periods and cultures made available and the clinic works with persons, the concept has a sociohistorical use, which follows them over time, and a clinical use, developed here, which describes their configuration in a particular life. This displacement makes the radicalization poststructuralist in lineage and postconstructionist in position, reorienting how narrative therapy conceives its object, listening, knowledge, agency, and change.

articles.title: Some Data Indicating that Editors and Reviewers Do Not Check Preregistrations during the Review Process
articles.authors: Moin Syed
articles.abstract: If a study is preregistered, but nobody checks it during review, does it mean anything? The purpose of this preregistered study was to better understand how editors and reviewers engage with preregistration plans during the review process. The article set was retrieved from the PLOS family of journals, which a) are cross-disciplinary, b) are open access, c) have a relatively high frequency of preregistered studies, and d) most importantly, in 2019 began publishing manuscript reviews alongside published articles. A total of 693 articles were identified via the initial search, which was reduced to 201 that met the review criteria. For each article, the review history was coded for whether editors or reviewers a) mentioned the preregistration, b) accessed the preregistration, and c) made specific mention of the relation between the preregistration and reporting in the paper. Analyses were conducted at the article level (i.e., did any reviewer or editor mention/access/compare; n = 201) and the editor/reviewer level (i.e., overall, how many editors/reviewers mention/access/compare; n = 689). At the article level, 43% of articles at least one editor/reviewer mentioned the preregistration, but in only 14% did they mention accessing the preregistration and in 10% did someone make a clear statement about the relation between the preregistration and the manuscript. In contrast, at the editor/reviewer level things look much worse, with only 18% mentioning preregistration, 5% reporting accessing the preregistration, and 3% discussing the relation between the preregistration and the manuscript. These data suggest very low levels of engagement with preregistrations during the review process, which undermines some of the primary goals of the practice.

articles.title: Counting on Suppression: Does Learning to Ignore Distractors Depend on Executive Resources? A Registered Report
articles.authors: Francisco Garre-Frutos; Miguel A. Vadillo; David Shanks; Francisco Vicente-Conesa
articles.abstract: Observers can learn to suppress the locations where salient distractors tend to appear, so that distractors at these locations are less likely to capture attention. This learned distractor suppression is thought to depend on an automatic mechanism that does not require working memory resources. However, previous dual-task studies in this literature have often asked participants to retain or manipulate information that was tested after search, which does not necessarily engage executive processes during learning. In the present study, we will test more directly whether learning to suppress a distractor location depends on executive resources. To do so, participants will perform an additional singleton task while counting the targets that contain a given line orientation, a concurrent executive task integrated into the search itself. We will compare this load group with a no-load control group that will perform the same task without the concurrent task. We hypothesise that the suppression effect will be smaller in the load group than in the control group (H1). Moreover, if this form of learning requires executive resources, the suppression effect could be absent in the load group (H2). The results will show whether learned distractor suppression is independent of executive resources, or whether previous null results reflect secondary tasks that left these resources available during search.

articles.title: DC-Debates: Difficulty-Calibrated Debate Transcripts as Stimuli for Scalable Oversight Research with Human Participants
articles.authors: Gabriel Recchia; Chatrik Singh Mangat; Suhasini Satish Rao; Sanika Khadkikar
articles.abstract: Approaches to scalable oversight involving human judges, such as AI safety via debate, will be more likely to achieve success if systematic errors in judgment can be minimized. Research on approaches to reducing this error, such as different ways of aggregating participant judgments or manipulating instructions to human participants, is more likely to generalise well if conducted using stimuli analogous to the kinds of stimuli that we expect strong trained AI debaters to generate. This requires well-designed transcripts that are difficult enough to leave room for interventions to improve judge accuracy, but tractable enough that an attentive judge has some hope of arriving at the correct answer. We describe the construction of 24 debate transcripts spanning 12 questions in three domains (astrophysics research, brainteasers, and reward-hacking evaluations) that assume an underlying recursive protocol, with section-level balancing across 11 stylistic and rhetorical dimensions. We report a preregistered between-subjects study with human judges (N = 1,282) which estimates per-transcript posterior difficulty on the logit scale and partitions the 24 transcripts into a four-tier ordinal difficulty matrix. Our results show that our stimuli span a range of difficulty levels, providing a calibrated stimulus pool for subsequent research. We also report several failure modes in which honest debaters did not bring judges to the correct answer despite faithful argumentation, including a recursive-protocol-specific failure in which the dishonest debater steers recursion onto the less important of two subclaims. All transcripts, judge instructions, and analysis code are released as supplementary materials to facilitate follow-up work.

articles.title: Defining Log Data Indicators for the Measurement of  Generic Critical Online Reasoning (GEN-COR)
articles.authors: Jannick Illmann; Daniel Baumartz; Philine Drake; Carolin Hahnel; Johannes Hartig; Carmen Köhler; Marcus Schrickel; Frank Goldhammer
articles.abstract:
Background: For higher education students, the Internet has become the most important source of information. Because of the vast amount of misleading or biased information on the Internet, it poses challenges students need specific skills for, which are described by Critical Online Reasoning (COR). Other studies on comparable literacy constructs employed closed information spaces and simulated online environments.
	Objectives: We identify log data indicators for one of COR’s facets, Online Information Acquisition (OIA), and accumulate them into a factor structure using an open online environment.
	Methods: 566 first-year students of three German universities logged into a virtual machine and completed a questionnaire consisting of tasks requiring an online search. Through logging their search behaviour, we extracted log events and combined them into indicators for OIA based on literature as well as our own developments. We then employed factor analysis to find their underlying structure.
	Results and Conclusions: We identified ten log data indicators for OIA, of which six could be accumulated into a factor structure. Despite our initial assumption of a single underlying factor, we found two factors for OIA, one concerning search term formulation and the other concerning behaviour on the search engine results page. This expands our knowledge about OIA and COR and shows the feasibility of using log data indicators for digital literacy research.

articles.title: Temporal associations between short-form video use and affective dynamics: A 14-day ecological momentary assessment among Chinese university students
articles.authors: Yu Gu; Wen Zheng; Johannes Thrul
articles.abstract: Short-form video use is associated with poor emotional well-being, yet its short-term associations with affect in daily life remain unclear. In a 14-day ecological momentary assessment study, 134 Chinese university students completed 17,514 surveys, yielding 14,899 complete same-day lag-1 transitions. Bayesian multilevel dynamic models separated within-person fluctuations from between-person differences and estimated associations of prior affect with subsequent interval use, interval use with end-of-interval affect, and daily use rate with affective dynamics. We identified several associations at the momentary timescale: 1) At the 90-minute reference interval, reported short-form video use was associated with 1.36 points lower positive affect (95% credible interval −2.36 to −0.39) and 1.47 points higher overall negative affect (0.59 to 2.40) on 0–100 scales; 2) Among occasions with prior non-zero negative affect, the 75th versus 25th percentile of its intensity corresponded to an increase of 1.74 percentage points in subsequent short-form video use probability (0.89 to 2.60). At the daily timescale: 1) Daily short-form video use rate was not associated with mean levels of either positive or negative affect; 2) Higher daily use rates were associated with slightly weaker positive-affect carryover and lower residual variability. In conclusion, our findings highlight the dynamic associations between short-form video use and affect across multiple timescales. These findings motivate further research using objective use logs and designs capable of supporting causal inference.

articles.title: Children spontaneously compute scalar implicatures
articles.authors: Ebru Evcen; David Barner
articles.abstract: A large developmental literature finds that children often fail to compute scalar implicatures, accepting underinformative descriptions such as, “Some of the horses jumped” when all of them did, or, “The bear took a cup or a plate” when he took both. Here, we argue that past studies find such failures because they do not evaluate children’s spontaneous interpretation of utterances, but instead ask how they interpret language when provided proffered “worlds” that children would not consider otherwise. We show that when children are allowed the chance to act upon their own spontaneous interpretation of utterances, they compute scalar implicatures in an adult-like fashion. Specifically, we tested children in two conditions: a standard Truth Value Judgment (TVJ) condition, similar to past studies, and a novel, two-phase Act-Out+TVJ condition in which children first acted on the utterance by coloring pictures before judging a puppet's action. In the act-out task children almost never colored both disjuncts after hearing “or” (Experiment 1) and rarely colored all four objects after hearing “some” (Experiment 2). More importantly, after acting out these interpretations, children computed scalar implicatures in an adult-like fashion, and significantly more often than children in the TVJ-only condition. These findings suggest that preschoolers spontaneously access relevant alternative utterances and compute scalar implicatures when allowed to generate their own interpretations before evaluating experimenter-provided worlds, and that previous studies underestimate this ability by artificially proffering irrelevant worlds.

articles.title: Attenuated Alcohol–Valence Congruency Effects in Abstinent Individuals With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Bipolar Implicit Association Test Study
articles.authors: Nicolás Guillermo González; Boris Vucotich; Ana Clara Alcici De Melo Viana Rocha; Lucia Alba-Ferrara
articles.abstract:
Alcohol-valence Implicit Association Tests (IATs) assess relative compatibility
between response mappings, but findings in alcohol use disorder (AUD) are mixed. We
examined alcohol-valence congruency effects in abstinent, treatment-engaged adults with
AUD using a shortened Spanish-language bipolar IAT. Thirty-four participants (17 with
AUD, abstinent for 2–24 months and receiving community-based treatment in Buenos Aires,
Argentina; 17 controls) classified alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverage words and positive
and negative valence words. Reaction times were analyzed using a 2 × 2 × 2 mixed ANOVA
(Congruency × Stimulus Type × Group). Responses were faster overall for the
alcohol-negative/non-alcohol-positive pairing than for the reverse pairing. Critically, the
Congruency × Group interaction was significant, F(1, 32) = 10.73, p = .003, ηp² = .251. The
mean congruency effect was 266.0 ms in controls and 83.2 ms in AUD. The corresponding
interaction in accuracy was not significant, and the reaction-time interaction remained
significant after natural-log transformation of participant-level mean reaction times. The
three-way Congruency × Stimulus Type × Group interaction was not significant. These
findings indicate an attenuated relative alcohol-valence congruency effect in abstinent AUD,
without identifying which individual associative components account for this difference.

articles.title: Can Intellectual Humility Reduce Ideological Conflict? Theory, Evidence, and Research Priorities
articles.authors: Jonah Koetke; Karina Schumann
articles.abstract: Ideological conflict threatens democracy and social cohesion worldwide. Although intergroup contact can reduce prejudice between ideological groups, significant barriers prevent effective contact. In this theoretical review, we propose that intellectual humility (IH)—the awareness of one’s intellectual limitations—may help overcome these barriers. We present a framework arguing that IH could promote effective contact through three pathways: (1) increasing other-focused cognitions and behaviors, (2) reducing reflexive defensiveness, and (3) reducing information bias. We review evidence drawn primarily from US horizontal affective polarization research that is consistent with this framework. We also outline four research priorities that are necessary for future work on IH and ideological conflict, including establishing causality through experimental designs, resolving measurement and conceptual ambiguities, testing generalizability across contexts and populations, and demonstrating real-world impact and scalability. This framework and research agenda provide a roadmap for investigating IH as a potential lever for improving intergroup relations across ideological divisions.

articles_hidden.title: Economic and social conservatism show a complex relationship with values of inequality and social control in an online US sample
articles_hidden.authors: Guy A. Lavender Forsyth; Ananish Chaudhuri; Quentin Atkinson
articles_hidden.abstract: Economically and socially conservative attitudes are frequently presented as stemming from distinct values about inequality and social control, respectively. However, existing research often relies on psychological scales, like Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) and Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA), that were not designed to measure values about inequality and social control directly, and which blur the boundary between values and attitudes. Here, we explore the relationship between political values and attitudes in an online USA sample (N=893), taking advantage of the new Dual Foundations Scale, which was specifically designed to measure inequality and social control values. Using multilevel Bayesian models to examine relationships at the level of individual attitudes, we find that, as predicted, values of inequality were positively associated with economic conservatism, and values about social control with social conservatism. However, associations varied across individual items, and social conservatism was overall less strongly associated with social control values than with inequality values and religious identification. Exploratory follow-up analyses indicate that whereas economically conservative attitudes cluster as expected with inequality values and SDO, socially conservative attitudes are not reliably related to social control values (or RWA’s Submission or Aggression subdimensions) and instead cluster with RWA Traditionalism, which is made up of items that some argue simply restate socially conservative attitudes. Our novel approach and findings therefore support some of the main claims of two-dimensional theories of ideology while challenging others, and suggest relationships between social conservatism, social control values, and authoritarianism are more complex than standard two-dimensional approaches to political ideology often assume.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Diagnostic Categories: Policy Implications of Dimensional Classification of Mental Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Aidan G.C. Wright; Christopher James Hopwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Debates about whether psychiatric classification of mental illness should shift from the current categories (i.e., you have a diagnosis or you do not) to dimensions (i.e., people all fall along a spectrum of severity) has intensified in recent years. The balance of evidence strongly favors dimensional models, and official diagnostic manuals are considering widespread adoption of dimensional systems for diagnosis. We consider what follows for policies that interface with mental health, drawing primarily on United States examples. Policies across law, insurance, disability, drug regulation, licensing, and education already combine diagnostic categories with eligibility standards defined by the relevant organizations. Dimensional classification systems will make the distinction between clinical description and policy driven decision rules more explicit. We argue that mental health symptoms and functional impairment should be assessed separately, and that policies should turn on evidence relevant to treatment need, daily functioning, and risk. We offer seven recommendations for developing, evaluating, and implementing such standards. Explicit thresholds of functioning for context-relevant impairment could improve policy without making a diagnostic label or numerical score the sole basis for granting services or restricting rights.

articles_hidden.title: Construct Emergence Tracing: From Meaning to Mechanism in Transformer Interpretability via Generative Psychometrics
articles_hidden.authors: Hudson Golino
articles_hidden.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) allow researchers and practitioners to develop and deploy systems that perform impressive feats such as generating coherent texts and answering questions across various domains. Yet, there is currently an interpretability problem regarding the internal representation of multidimensional psychological constructs (e.g., personality traits) throughout multiple layers of deep neural networks. Here, we propose Construct Emergence Tracing (CET), a novel methodology to address this problem. CET utilizes ideas from Generative Psychometrics to trace the emergence of concepts from high-level meaning to underlying mechanisms. CET consists of Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis combined with three complementary indices reflecting the quality of representation (semantic coherence via normalized mutual information; NMI, entropy-based organization structure via Total Entropy Fit Index; TEFI, and topological compressibility via a compression-based proxy for Kolmogorov Complexity; KC). CET also computes a weighted composite of the above three indices in order to derive a metric named Representational Maturity (RM). We applied CET to fourteen LM models ranging from nominal sizes of 117 million to 32 billion parameters. We utilized a fixed design of five items per attribute representing the five attributes of grandiose narcissism and yielded a total of 9,801,000 network estimates across recorded states, embedding dimensions, and repeated item samples. Results show that across architectures construct recovery generally increases from early to intermediate states. However, its initiation, amplitude, alignment with different metrics, and termination vary considerably across models. Across Qwen2.5-Instruct, overall mean NMI followed a monotonic increase based on nominal model size from 0.504 (0.5B) to 0.653 (32B). This trend did not replicate for selected peak values or output layer retention. Furthermore, the final state was divided into two distinct patterns of behaviors: (a) five models showed zero or close-to-zero mean NMI (GPT-2, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B); (b) nine models maintained final state mean NMI within 0.504-0.777 range. Lastly, we observed no consistent convergence in the optimal layers regarding peak semantic coherence, optimal entropy fit, and maximal representational maturity. Overall, we demonstrated that both the number of parameters and the extraction from the output layer alone do not suffice in capturing abstract representations inside LMs. Through CET, researchers and practitioners obtain macro-level estimations of construct organization trajectories across different layers.

articles_hidden.title: A review of perceived social traits in AI-generated hyperrealistic human faces
articles_hidden.authors: Dalia Israel; Genevieve Quek; Manuel Varlet; Tijl Grootswagers
articles_hidden.abstract: Advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) produce synthetic human faces that are difficult to distinguish from photographs of real people. Because social impressions from faces form rapidly and can influence consequential judgements, the growing realism of AI-generated faces raises questions about how these faces are socially perceived. This review synthesises evidence from 10 empirical studies examining whether AI-generated faces are evaluated differently from real faces and what may account for these differences. Across the reviewed studies, AI-generated faces receive more favourable social evaluations than real faces, including higher ratings of trustworthiness and attractiveness, while familiarity also emerges as a component of their perception. These patterns are consistent with established face-perception research showing that faces perceived as more typical tend to receive more favourable social evaluations. AI-generated faces may disproportionately reflect such characteristics, including greater averageness or typicality. However, appearance alone does not determine these judgements: disclosure, labelling, and beliefs about artificiality can weaken or alter otherwise favourable impressions. Overall, social responses to AI-generated faces appear to reflect an interaction between perceptual characteristics and beliefs about origin. The central challenge is no longer only whether AI-generated faces can pass as human, but how people who do not exist can shape real social judgements.

articles_hidden.title: Mitigating Retest Effects in High-Frequency Cognitive Assessment Data: A Tutorial on the Bayesian Double Exponential Model in Stan
articles_hidden.authors: Yanling Li; Joachim Vandekerckhove; Grace J. Chen; Martin Sliwinski; Zita Oravecz
articles_hidden.abstract: In this tutorial, we give a comprehensive, step-by-step guide for implementing the Bayesian Double Exponential Model (BDEM) in the popular Bayesian software Stan. The BDEM is a statistical tool designed to disentangle retest effects from true longitudinal cognitive change and to quantify individual differences in high-frequency repeated cognitive assessment data, typically collected in everyday settings. We give step-by-step guidelines for fitting BDEM in Stan and also describe implementations in PyMC and JAGS in an online supplement. Finally, we provide a real data example to highlight the unique inferences that can be drawn with our approach. The goal of this tutorial is to equip researchers with the necessary tools to apply advanced multilevel models of cognitive change and retest learning in high-frequency assessment designs.

articles_hidden.title: Inference-Time Self-Guidance for Conversational Safety in Delusion-Related Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: David Piterman; Elad Refoua; Hadar Dery; Gunther Meinlschmidt; Ziv Ben-Zion; Kfir Bar; Zohar Elyoseph
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychologically sensitive conversations, where repeated affirmation may reinforce delusion-related beliefs and associated risk. Inference-time self-guidance, in which a model generates conversation-specific guidance for subsequent responses without parameter updates, may offer an approach to conversational safety, but its utility in delusion-related interactions remains unclear.
Objective: To develop and evaluate conversation-specific inference-time self-guidance for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.
Methods: In this preregistered study, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash completed 16 Psychosis-Bench scenarios under Baseline and three self-guidance conditions: response rules, contrastive examples, and short-horizon consequence simulation. The fully crossed design yielded 192 conversations and 2,304 assistant turns. A separate automated judge scored Delusion Confirmation (DCS), Harm Enablement (HES), and Safety Intervention (SIS) using published Psychosis-Bench rubrics. Analyses compared benchmark-defined Explicit and Implicit risk-cue scenarios and examined whether self-guidance reduced this gap.
Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10–2.17). At Baseline, explicit risk cues elicited significantly greater SIS than matched implicit cues, whereas cue-type differences in DCS and HES were not significant. Self-guidance did not significantly attenuate the explicit–implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Conclusions: Model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior during standardized scripted escalation without parameter updates. These findings support further evaluation of inference-time self-guidance for delusion-related conversational safety, particularly when risk is communicated indirectly.

articles_hidden.title: Attentional Bias as an Intermediate Mechanism Linking Executive Dysfunction to Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD
articles_hidden.authors: Mahdieh Vaezbarenji; Edmund Sonuga-Barke
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is increasingly recognised as involving persistent difficulties in emotion regulation alongside well-established executive dysfunction. However, the cognitive mechanisms linking executive control impairments to emotional dysregulation remain insufficiently integrated within existing theoretical models. The present conceptual review proposes that attentional bias toward emotionally salient stimuli represents an intermediate cognitive-affective mechanism linking executive dysfunction to emotional dysregulation in ADHD. Drawing on evidence from attentional processing, executive control, affective neuroscience, and neurobiological models of ADHD, the review argues that impaired top-down prefrontal regulatory systems reduce the ability to suppress stimulus-driven attentional capture by emotionally salient information. Consequently, biased attentional allocation may amplify emotional reactivity, prolong engagement with negative affective stimuli, and interfere with adaptive emotion regulation processes. Neurobiologically, disrupted functional connectivity between prefrontal regulatory networks and salience-processing systems, including the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and ventral striatum, may contribute to both attentional and emotional dysregulation in ADHD. The review further discusses theoretical and clinical implications of this framework, including the potential value of interventions targeting attentional control and emotional attentional processing. Limitations of the current evidence base and directions for future longitudinal and neurobiological research are also considered. Conceptualising attentional bias within a broader neurocognitive framework may provide a more integrated and mechanistically coherent account of emotional dysregulation in ADHD.

articles_hidden.title: Neural representational changes after category learning across sensory modalities: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Anthony Cruz; Madeline Bloomberg; John Paul Minda
articles_hidden.abstract: Category learning is a fundamental mechanism underlying concept formation, yet the extent to which it induces stable neural representational changes across sensory modalities remains unclear. This preregistered systematic review assesses functional neuroimaging studies that examined whether experience with a novel category structure alters the brain’s responses to the newly categorized stimuli, specifically outside of active categorization. Across 26 experiments meeting inclusion criteria, 81% reported learning-related changes in neural representations of stimuli following category acquisition. These effects were observed using fMRI, EEG, and MEG in a variety of paradigms. Eighteen visual and seven auditory studies tended to find these changes in higher-order cortical regions associated with object and speech processing. Other kinds of evidence were sparse. The single olfactory study found altered patterns of connectivity following learning. A minority of studies (5/26) found no evidence of task-independent representational changes, with task-dependent or null results being reported. The current state of the literature suggests that category learning can produce durable changes in the neural representations of stimuli in the brain, with the loci and nature of these changes varying across modalities. Limitations of the existing literature and suggestions for future work are highlighted.

articles_hidden.title: Decoding Affect: A Computational Model of Affective Adaptation and Construction
articles_hidden.authors: Haijiao Cui; Liu-Fang Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective construction and adaptation are complementary processes through which affective value is generated and evolves over time. Although prior research has identified key determinants of these processes, including reference points, stimulus inherent value, attention, negativity bias, adaptation rate, and time, a unified framework that quantifies how these factors interact and jointly shape affect remains lacking, leaving important nonlinear affective phenomena insufficiently explained. We propose the Attention-Reference Interaction Adaptation (ARIA) framework, which formalizes affective valuation as an attention-gated dual-reference integration process that evaluates current sensory inputs relative to both prior experience and allostatic set-points. By specifying how value salience and negativity bias jointly govern attention allocation and adaptation rate, ARIA suggests that relativity and asymmetry (two foundational properties of affective valuation) arise from a shared attentional mechanism. Consequently, these properties are contingent, dynamically coupled, and conditionally reducible, rather than fixed, independent, and irreducible axioms as assumed in classical behavioral economic theories. Furthermore, we map ARIA's computational components onto reward and interoceptive prediction errors, capturing how external and internal discrepancies jointly drive the construction of affective experience. Through numerical simulations and an initial empirical test, we show that ARIA reproduces classic affective phenomena, such as exponential decay, affective after-reactions, and alliesthesia, while also accounting for anomalous patterns, including cases in which environmental improvements fail to elicit pleasure and conditions under which inherently positive stimuli adapt more slowly than negative ones. Ultimately, ARIA offers a tractable computational framework for explaining affective dynamics and generating testable predictions about well-being and environmental experience.

articles_hidden.title: MDMA as a Means of Augmenting Exposure Therapy in the Context of Social Anxiety Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Jason B Luoma; M. Kati Lear; Brian Pilecki
articles_hidden.abstract: Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) presents a significant barrier to social and work functioning, and while exposure therapy has been a cornerstone of treatment, its effectiveness varies across individuals. This paper discusses how 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) may be used to enhance the effectiveness of an exposure-based intervention in SAD treatment. MDMA, known for its capacity to enhance feelings of social safeness, may enhance exposure therapy through a variety of mechanisms such as reducing safety behaviors, increasing contact with cues for core SAD fears, increasing expectancy violations, and increasing willingness. We explore the neurobiological and psychological underpinnings relevant to this augmentation strategy, particularly MDMA’s modulation of serotonin and dopamine pathways and its tendency to elicit self-transcendent positive emotions such as love, compassion, and gratitude. We also discuss recent findings suggesting that MDMA may open a window of neuroplasticity after administration during which effective exposure practice may have larger effects. To provide an illustration of these concepts, we describe how these ideas are being used to guide in vivo and imaginal exposure interventions as part of our clinical trial of MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder.  Ethical considerations, potential risks, and a framework for future empirical studies to test this theory are outlined. This approach could potentially offer a more profound and enduring therapeutic impact for those struggling with SAD, suggesting a promising area for further research.

articles_hidden.title: AX-CPT Measures Show Good Reliability and Shared Variance, but Raise Concerns About Their Validity
articles_hidden.authors: Niels Oliver Kempkens; Alodie Rey-Mermet
articles_hidden.abstract: Attentional control refers to the ability to maintain a goal and goal-relevant information in the face of distraction. Previous research has highlighted the lack of reliability and shared variance in attentional-control measures. This may result from the heterogeneity of the control processes induced by the tasks. The aim of the present study was to reduce or control for this heterogeneity in two ways. First, we used one task – the AX-CPT – with different stimulus materials (letters, words, dot patterns, matrices, and pictures). In this task, a target response is required in trials where two specific stimuli occur in sequence (e.g., the letter “A” followed by the letter “X”). In all other trials, a non-target response is required. Second, we distinguished between proactive control (goal maintenance) and reactive control (goal reactivation) by computing separate indices for each process. Using data from 667 young adults, we obtained good reliability for most indices. Confirmatory factor analysis identified models with factors representing shared variance across stimulus materials. In a subsequent analysis, we bypassed the indices by modeling proactive and reactive control directly from error rates and response times. Using a bifactor modeling approach, we found shared variance across stimulus materials for error rates only. However, in both analyses, the pattern of latent correlations contradicted the expectations. For example, a positive and very high correlation was observed between indices representing proactive and reactive control. Overall, these findings raise concerns about the validity of AX-CPT measures.

articles_hidden.title: Retrieval-Augmented Virtual Patients for Eating Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Carlo Smaniotto Mantovani; Wagner de Lara Machado; Bolivar Ramos Cibils Filho; Regis Kopper; Gabriel Balke dos Santos; Joao Ricardo Nickenig Vissoci; Márcio Sarroglia Pinho
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Language models can generate fluent virtual patient dialogue, but its clinical plausibility requires evaluation. Objective: We describe a locally deployed simulator for anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder and examine the perceived realism of its responses. Method: A Unity application links a three-dimensional avatar to Llama 3 8B. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) configuration uses Nomic Embed Text and ChromaDB to retrieve clinical material. Six raters from psychology or nutrition assessed 45 Brazilian Portuguese responses to 15 questions under three conditions: Llama 3 8B without RAG, Llama 3 8B with RAG, and GPT-4o. Each response received six ratings on a five-point realism scale, yielding 270 ratings. Comparisons were descriptive, and agreement was assessed using quadratically weighted Gwet’s AC2. Results: Mean realism was 3.81 without RAG, 3.76 with RAG, and 4.65 for GPT-4o. Observed agreement was 83.5%, with AC2 = .60. Qualitative comments emphasized clinical plausibility concerns without RAG and language quality concerns with RAG; error frequencies were not quantified. Conclusions: RAG was not associated with a higher overall realism mean in this response set. Clinical plausibility and linguistic naturalness warrant separate assessment in a comparison that controls generation settings. The study did not evaluate avatar effects, multi-turn coherence, safety, or learning outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptivity complicates causality: How to evaluate the effects of adaptive support
articles_hidden.authors: Jasmin Breitwieser; Mirijam Schaaf; Garvin Brod
articles_hidden.abstract: Digital technologies make it possible to adapt the level of support to students’ behavior. However, determining what level is optimal for each student is methodologically challenging: If adaptations depend on prior behavior, adaptivity decisions are not fully randomized, which complicates causal inference. We present a methodological approach based on sequential experimental designs and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to evaluate adaptivity decisions. We illustrate this approach in a mobile intervention promoting frequent vocabulary study. Students received planning prompts during a 20-day first-stage intervention, followed by an adapted prompting frequency in the second stage. Using a DAG, we formalized causal assumptions, identified confounding, and adjusted for it. The results illustrate the importance of this methodological approach to obtain valid causal conclusions: an unadjusted analysis would have led to the incorrect conclusion that scheduling more prompts leads to reduced study activity. This underscores the importance of making adaptivity decisions in an evidence-based way.

articles_hidden.title: Subjective and objective socioeconomic status as predictors of midlife cognition in the rural Deep South: the Bogalusa Heart Study
articles_hidden.authors: Jade E. Jenkins; Amy Thierry; Ileana De Anda-Duran; Shakira Suglia; Lydia Bazzano; Owen Carmichael
articles_hidden.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Lifecourse socioeconomic conditions influence Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) risk. Higher objective socioeconomic status (O-SES) is consistently associated with better later life cognition and lower ADRD risk. One’s perception of their socioeconomic status, or subjective socioeconomic status (S-SES), is a robust predictor of myriad health outcomes. However, it’s utility as a predictor of cognition in aging populations is not well characterized and has yet to be investigated in the Deep South, a historically underrepresented region characterized by socioeconomic disadvantage and elevated ADRD risk. 
METHODS: O-SES and S-SES were examined as predictors of cognition in the Bogalusa Heart Study. We derived O-SES using confirmatory factor analysis and measured S-SES using the country ladder from the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status. Exploratory analyses were conducted to test for potential effect measure modification by sex and race. 
RESULTS: O-SES, but not S-SES, was associated with cognition in the full sample. Exploratory analyses revealed a small positive association between S-SES and cognition only for White men, which was attenuated after accounting for O-SES. The relationship between O-SES and cognition was not modified by sex and race.
DISCUSSION: Our finding that higher O-SES is associated with better cognition is consistent with extensive evidence. However, we did not replicate previously found associations between S-SES and cognition observed in other older populations and with numerous other health outcomes. Given the paucity of research in the rural Deep South, more work is needed to understand S-SES and ADRD risk in this setting.

articles_hidden.title: Sequential Priming Builder: A Free, No-Code Tool  for Implementing Sequential Priming Paradigms
articles_hidden.authors: Yubo Zhou; Jiaxi Ye; Wen Song; Zihan Yang; Mo Han; Wenlu Du; Lu Zang; Xi Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: Sequential priming tasks are a family of methods widely used in psychology. However, implementing sequential priming tasks typically requires custom programming and deployment through third-party platforms. To address these challenges, we developed a free tool that requires no coding skills — the Sequential Priming Builder (SP-Builder: spbuilder.org). This tool uses a graphical user interface that enables researchers to easily build different types of sequential priming tasks, which can be integrated into the widely used online survey platform Qualtrics. We assessed the tool’s reliability and timing accuracy in online environments across two studies. In Study 1, we showed that it correctly presented the predefined stimulus sequence and accurately recorded elapsed time. We also evaluated the timing error of stimulus presentation under conditions where typical online participant interactions were simulated. We conducted Study 2 using a preregistered Affect Misattribution Procedure (AMP; N = 92), a widely used sequential priming task. We built the study with SP-Builder, and the results replicated the published findings.

articles_hidden.title: Body image in relation to ADHD and ADHD traits: A mixed-methods scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Phaedra Longhurst; Lauren Makin; Fidan Turk; Helena Lewis-Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Accumulating evidence suggests associations between ADHD, negative body image, and 
disordered eating; however, relatively little is known about how body image has been 
conceptualised, assessed, and experienced. This mixed-methods scoping review aimed to 
map and synthesise existing research examining body image in relation to ADHD and ADHD 
traits. Seven databases (Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, and 
Scopus) and two grey literature sources (PsyArXiv and ProQuest) were searched from 
inception to September 2026. Data were charted iteratively and synthesised descriptively 
and narratively. Twenty-seven studies (25 quantitative, two qualitative) published between 
1995 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. All studies were based in Westernised contexts, 
with most employing cross-sectional designs. ADHD was predominantly assessed using
symptom-based measures and/or diagnostic status, while body image was most commonly 
assessed using subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory. Quantitative studies primarily 
examined associations between ADHD and negative body image, with some evidence of 
greater negative body image in ADHD. However, findings were inconsistent across studies, 
particularly following adjustment for covariates (e.g., co-occurring psychopathology). The 
literature predominantly adopted pathology-oriented conceptualisations of body image, with 
no studies examining positive body image and limited exploration of lived 
experiences. Further gaps were identified in methodological approaches, the 
conceptualisation and measurement of body image and ADHD, and the representation of 
diverse populations. Reliance on predominantly neurotypical-derived conceptualisations and 
measurement tools not validated among ADHD samples raises concerns about their 
validity. Future research should prioritise participatory approaches to advance an inclusive, 
neuro-affirming understanding of body image among the ADHD population.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological dimensions of wise reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Veronica Diveica; Bri Susanna Darboh; Roni Setton; Gary R. Turner; R. Nathan Spreng
articles_hidden.abstract: Wise reasoning is an adaptive capacity associated with wellbeing and pro-sociality across the lifespan, yet why some individuals reason more wisely than others remains unclear. We examined factors associated with individual differences in wise reasoning across five major psychological domains, and tested whether these associations differ between younger and older adults. A sample of 179 younger and 161 older adults completed a performance-based measure of wise reasoning, two self-report measures of wisdom traits, and a comprehensive battery assessing autobiographical memory, crystallized and fluid cognition, personality, affect, and social functioning. Greater wise reasoning capacity was associated with the richness of autobiographical recollection, better crystallized cognition, greater openness to experience, and better emotion recognition, but not affective dispositions. Cognitive performance accounted for more variance in wise reasoning than any other psychological domain. A data-driven analysis further revealed that wise reasoning capacity is best characterized by a multivariate pattern of covarying factors spanning psychological domains. Although most associations were similar across age groups, some evidence of age-related moderation emerged, including stronger associations with autobiographical memory vividness among younger adults and openness to experience among older adults. The correlates of wise reasoning did not fully generalize to self-reported wisdom traits, which were associated primarily with self-reported personality and affective dispositions. These findings advance an integrated account of the psychological foundations of wise reasoning across adulthood, highlighting their multidimensional nature, relative stability across the adult lifespan, and the key roles of autobiographical memory and crystallized cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion dysregulation in everyday life among children with ADHD: A cross-cultural qualitative study of parents’ accounts in Belgium and China
articles_hidden.authors: Canmei Xu; Lisa B Thorell; Mariette Huizinga; Ruwen Liang; Dieter Baeyens
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional dysregulation (ED) is frequently observed among children with ADHD, yet little is known about how it unfolds in everyday life, particularly across cultural contexts. This qualitative study examined ED in primary school-aged children with ADHD in a Western cultural context (Belgium) and an Eastern cultural context (China). We interviewed 20 parents in each country and analyzed the interviews using meta-theme analysis. Across both groups, the interview accounts reflected a recurring sequence captured by five interrelated themes: context-specific triggers, emotional overload, dysregulated emotional expression, relational impact, and perceived effects on children’s self-image over time. The groups’ accounts differed in some of the situations parents described as triggers and in how parents interpreted emotional episodes and their consequences. These findings suggest that assessment and support for children with ADHD should take into account how families in different cultural contexts identify emotional triggers and interpret emotional episodes and their consequences.

articles_hidden.title: The cortical representation of materials and their properties
articles_hidden.authors: Hua-Chun Sun; Martin N Hebart; Filipp Schmidt; Roland Fleming
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceiving materials like metal, wood or soil is essential for many everyday tasks, yet we still understand little about how materials are represented in the brain. Here we report the most comprehensive mapping of neural representations of materials and their properties to date. In an event-related fMRI design over multiple sessions, six participants viewed every image in the STUFF dataset—which includes 200 different material categories—14 times each, yielding precise estimates of cortical responses. We compared these responses with 36 ‘core dimensions’ of material perception derived from >1.8 million perceptual similarity judgments on the same image set. This revealed ‘cortical feature maps’ of activity associated with each dimension. Most maps spanned large swaths of cortex, indicating a highly distributed and multiplexed representation. Multidimensional scaling revealed systematic relationships between the maps, with >95% of the variance between maps accounted for by just six axes.
