Despite this, for 35 of the 36 core dimensions, feature values could be decoded from brain activity patterns, and in pairwise comparisons, material categories could be decoded with 88.9% accuracy. Together our findings reveal a highly distributed multidimensional material representation that supports the read-out of both properties and categories of materials.

articles_hidden.title: How to Measure Victimhood and Moral Judgment with the Theory of Dyadic Morality
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Kubin; Kurt Gray
articles_hidden.abstract: The Theory of Dyadic Morality (TDM) argues that moral condemnation revolves around intuitive perceptions of victimization. We provide a curated collection of items for measuring moral judgment and perceived victimization, organized around one question: “From someone’s perspective, who is victimizing whom, how, and to what extent?” Each part of the question connects to a core element of our moral psychology, including the dyad itself (an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable victim), the continuum of perceived victimization (mild to severe), different kinds of victimization (e.g., physical violence versus spiritual suffering), and the important worldviews that shape perceived victimization (e.g., cultural and politics). We show how classic paradigms, from moral dilemmas to moral dumbfounding, can be measured with TDM, and we outline future directions, including how TDM can align artificial intelligence with human moral judgment.

articles_hidden.title: Recovery Capital, Structural Barriers, and Wellbeing Among Adults in Addiction Recovery: Findings from the Life in Recovery Survey in Spain
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Serrano-Pastor; Sylvia Georgieva; Alfredo Zarco Alpuente; Ângela Maria Teixeira Leite; Paula Samper-Garcia; Jose-Antonio Giménez-Costa
articles_hidden.abstract:
Understanding how personal, social, and structural conditions shape recovery capital is important for explaining differences in addiction recovery and wellbeing. This study examined strengths and barriers during active addiction and recovery and their associations with addiction complexity, recovery trajectories, social and structural conditions, perceived change, and wellbeing. A cross-sectional national survey included 1,598 adults in recovery in Spain who completed the Spanish-adapted Life in Recovery survey and measures of social and living conditions, quality of life, and harmony in life. Analyses included paired t tests, correlations, group comparisons, and hierarchical regression models. Participants retrospectively reported substantially more strengths (mean difference = 4.23, d = 1.03) and fewer barriers (mean difference = -4.74, d = 1.33) in recovery than during active addiction. Strength growth and barrier reduction were modestly associated (r = -.29), supporting their interpretation as related but distinct dimensions of recovery capital. Higher strengths in recovery were associated with more consolidated self-identified recovery stages, earlier problem identification and recovery initiation, use of multiple recovery pathways, and greater satisfaction with social and living conditions (R² = .128). Barriers were more strongly patterned by structural conditions, including employment, housing, and perceived economic situation (R² = .070). Higher strengths, fewer current barriers, and greater perceived barrier reduction were associated with better quality of life (R² = .092) and harmony in life (R² = .097), while women reported lower wellbeing after adjustment. The findings support a contextual and multidimensional understanding of recovery capital and highlight the importance of strengthening personal and social resources while addressing persistent material and structural barriers in recovery-oriented care.
Keywords: Addiction Recovery; Recovery Capital; Structural Barriers; Wellbeing; Life in Recovery; Recovery-Oriented Care.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Distance between Geographic Regions is associated with Lower Mobility, Weaker Democracy, and Increased Risk of Civil Conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Cindel J. M. White; Michael Muthukrishna
articles_hidden.abstract: Stable nations require strangers to coordinate and cooperate despite cultural differences. articles_hidden.title: Private Practitioners’ Use and Perceptions of Digital Mental Health Tools to Support Evidence-based Youth Psychotherapy
articles_hidden.authors: Josephine Halporn; John Parkhurst; Galen D. McNeil; Ruben G. Martinez; Ren Mondesir; Tierney McMahon; Ashley A. Knapp; Guo Sisi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mental health clinicians in private practice represent approximately half of the outpatient workforce. Clinicians in this environment have more global negative attitudes toward implementing evidence-based treatments (EBTs), despite the proven efficacy of EBTs in treating children and adolescents. Digital mental health (DMH) tools may help streamline EBT implementation, thus reducing demands on clinicians. However, little is known about how clinicians in this group perceive and use DMH tools with youth. 

Objective: This mixed methods study examined how clinicians in private practice currently use and perceive DMH tools. 

Method: Explanatory sequential design included survey data collection from 79 master’s- and doctoral-level licensed clinicians in two large, diverse urban regions within the U.S. Qualitative interviews were completed subsequently with 15 clinicians for purposes of thematic analysis. 

Results: More than half of survey participants endorsed currently using DMH tools (60.9%, n = 39) or being open to doing so (34.4%, n = 22). Those already open to and experienced in EBTs viewed DMH tools most favorably. Qualitative findings provided key insights into how clinicians are using DMH tools, as well as facilitators and barriers to their use.

Conclusions: DMH tools are being used to support elements of EBTs, and could reduce time spent out of session on tracking, preparation, and documentation for private practice clinicians. Future research should address barriers identified here in user-centered design processes with this group.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive changes after Covid-19 infection in the UK Biobank dataset
articles_hidden.authors: Josefina Weinerova; Andrew Reid; Denis Schluppeck; Roni Tibon
articles_hidden.abstract: SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for the Covid-19 pandemic, has been shown to have an impact on cognitive function, but the specific areas affected remain unclear. Cognitive changes in participants who recovered from Covid-19 (N=1085, 51-82 years) were compared to those of control participants tested before the pandemic and after the pandemic outbreak (pandemic control group, N=1011, 51-82 years) and to those of a second control group that underwent both testing sessions before the pandemic (pre-pandemic control group, N= 2360, 49-82 years). In accordance with our predictions, we found an effect of Covid-19 on associative memory, such that participants who underwent Covid-19 infection showed a decrease in performance compared to both control groups, conceptually replicating our previous results obtained with another dataset (Weinerova et al., 2025). Contrary to our predictions, however, we did not find an effect of Covid-19 on executive function, problem solving and language. This study provides valuable insights into the nature of cognitive changes after Covid-19 infection which may inform public health professionals and policy makers.

articles_hidden.title: Reliability Estimation and Reporting Practices in Ambulatory Assessments and Other Intensive Longitudinal Designs: A Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas B. Neubauer; Jean-Paul Snijder-Steinhilber
articles_hidden.abstract: Intensive longitudinal designs (e.g., ambulatory assessment, daily diaries) are an increasingly popular tool to examine individuals’ experiences in their everyday lives. Previous work suggests that level-specific reliability of measures in these designs is often not reported, which complicates the development and refinement of questionnaires for these designs. The present meta-analysis examined reliability reporting practices in a random sample of 500 peer-reviewed articles (535 studies) published between 2015 and 2024. Researchers should routinely report within- and between-person reliability separately, or justify its absence, to enable cumulative measurement development in intensive longitudinal research.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Dynamic Risks: Outcome Monitoring and Evaluation under Escalating Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Corinna Lorenz; Nicola Kristina Ferdinand
articles_hidden.abstract:
Real-world risk-taking unfolds through sequences of decisions where stakes escalate incrementally. Yet most ERP research examines isolated outcomes, leaving neural processing of accumulating risk poorly understood. We developed an ERP-adapted Columbia Card Task enabling precise temporal analysis of feedback processing across consecutive outcomes, systematically manipulating gain amounts, loss amounts, and loss
probability while recording EEG in 25 participants. We measured early outcome detection via the feedbackrelated negativity (FRN) and reward positivity (RewP) and later evaluative processing via the P3b.

Early outcome processing tentatively depended on the potential loss amount. FRN amplitudes differentiated between
positive and negative outcomes when large losses were at stake but not when losses were small, an effect carried by more pronounced responses to negative outcomes under large losses. The RewP showed a similar but less well supported pattern. Gain amount and loss probability did not modulate early components, and we found no evidence that they changed across the feedback sequence. In contrast, the P3b was larger for negative than for positive outcomes, and this difference increased across the feedback sequence as risk accumulated, without evidence for a dependence on the stakes. Exploratory analyses did not provide consistent evidence that individual risk propensity modulated these patterns.

With early processing scaling with the consequences at stake and later evaluation increasingly focusing on negative outcomes as the feedback sequence progresses, these findings suggest that outcome monitoring under escalating risk is not a fixed response to outcome valence.

articles_hidden.title: Powering Up Cognitive Psychology: Comparing Statistical Methods for Reaction Time Data Using Virtual Experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Federico D'Atri; Mateusz Hohol; Carlo Fantoni; Leonardo Egidi; Lilly Roth; Krzysztof Cipora
articles_hidden.abstract: Generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) are increasingly used to analyze reaction time (RT) data in cognitive psychology. Yet, whether they outperform linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) or t-tests on aggregated data in realistic experimental settings remains unclear. In this preregistered simulation study, we systematically compared three types of GLMMs – a Gamma GLMM, an Inverse Gaussian GLMM, and a novel Probit GLMM – to LMMs and the t-test on aggregated data. As the main performance metric, we introduced adjusted power, a measure that adjusts statistical power to equalize methods in terms of confidence interval coverage. To this end, we used virtual experiments derived from five large datasets: three from numerical cognition experiments investigating the SNARC effect (Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes), and two from inhibitory control tasks. Across 1,480,000 simulations covering 36 configurations and including RTs from over 2,000 participants, we found that Gamma and Probit GLMMs outperform LMMs and the t-test on average, with the Probit GLMM showing a particular advantage for detecting the SNARC effect. However, no single method dominates across all configurations: performance depends substantially on the dataset and effect considered, and some mixed-effects models require robust error estimation to provide adequate coverage at small sample sizes. Furthermore, a meta-simulation supported the virtual experiments approach, yielding performance estimates consistent with ground-truth benchmarks from fully parametric data-generating processes. To make these findings actionable, we provide the interactive Shiny app Powering Up Cognitive Psychology, which allows researchers to explore the results and select statistical methods suited to their experimental context.

articles_hidden.title: How real is virtual? A test of episodic memory with a shelf task
articles_hidden.authors: Corinna Martarelli; pauline Berthouzoz; Laura Rotheichner; Dejan Popic
articles_hidden.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) has been proposed as a bridge between laboratory studies and real-world behavior, offering both high experimental control and ecological validity. However, studies directly comparing virtual and real-world replicas remain scarce. The present study investigated three experimental conditions—IVR, non-immersive VR (N-IVR), and Reality—focusing on subjective experiences and episodic memory performance. Participants (N = 156) were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions and completed a Shelf Task involving two encoding sessions in which they placed 8 objects on a shelf per session, followed by two recall sessions 10 minutes later. After encoding, participants rated subjective experiences, including spatial presence (self-location and action possibilities), similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and game mechanics. Overall, IVR approximated real-world experience more closely than N-IVR. Ratings of action possibilities and similarity to daily life in IVR matched Reality, and IVR elicited higher enjoyment than both N-IVR and Reality. Some differences remained: self-location and game mechanics favored Reality, and cybersickness was unique to IVR, though at low levels. Memory performance revealed robust session × condition effects. In Session 1, IVR recall lagged behind N-IVR and Reality, suggesting initial challenges with IVR encoding. By Session 2, IVR performance improved markedly, reaching levels comparable to N-IVR for free recall and to both Reality and N-IVR for spatial recall. These findings highlight both the promise and limitations of IVR: it can closely approximate real-world experience and memory performance over repeated exposure, but subjective and embodied aspects of reality are not fully replicated. The results have implications for experimental and applied cognitive assessment, as well as clinical and training contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Auditory-perceptual deficits and speech illusions are associated with psychotomimesis in an NMDA receptor antagonist model of schizophrenia
articles_hidden.authors: Ursule Taujanskaite; Georges Iskandar; Vaughan Bell; Sunjeev Kamboj
articles_hidden.abstract: Hallucinations are a core symptom of psychosis. Predictive processing accounts suggest that hallucinations arise from an imbalance between sensory evidence and prior expectations. Given the role of glutamatergic dysfunction in psychosis, the NMDA receptor antagonist nitrous oxide (N2O) may provide a model for investigating hallucinatory experiences. This pre-registered study (https://osf.io/4jhsx examined the effects of N2O on subjective and behavioural indices of psychosis-like (hallucinatory) phenomena. Healthy participants were randomised to 50%-N2O (n=80) or medical-air (n=40) and completed the Psychotomimetic States Inventory (PSI) before and during gas inhalation. False alarms, hits, and exploratory signal detection indices from the white noise (speech illusions) task were compared between N2O and medical-air. Mediation of drug effects on canonical signal detection metrics – perceptual sensitivity and response bias – via change in psychotomimesis (ΔPSI) and sedation was also examined. N2O administration was associated with fewer hits but no change in false alarms, reflected in reduced perceptual sensitivity and more conservative response bias. Larger ΔPSI was associated with more false alarms in the N2O group; ΔPSI (particularly positive psychotomimesis; ΔPSI-Positive) also mediated the effect of drug condition on perceptual sensitivity, while sedation and negative psychotomimesis did not have a reliable indirect role. However, the unexpected pattern of reduced perceptual sensitivity and conservative response bias under N2O challenges the notion that reduced perceptual sensitivity following NMDA-receptor antagonism would necessarily lead to hallucination-like responding.

articles_hidden.title: Do policy “packages” increase public  support for climate policies?
articles_hidden.authors: Yu Shuang Gan; Lorraine Whitmarsh; Lois Player; Yasmin Sachdev; Alice Moseley
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper addresses the paradox that most effective policy measures (e.g., coercive or ‘push’ policies) are often least supported by the public who prefer less intrusive, but also less effective measures (e.g., ‘pull’ policies that merely encourage behaviour change). Consequently, there is an onus on policymakers to create combinations of policies, or policy ‘packages’, that are both effective and publicly acceptable. Using evidence from two UK-based surveys, we examined the extent to which different combinations of climate policies are accepted across different population segments, policy domains, and conditions. We found some evidence that combinations of push-pull policies are more supported than push-only polices, but not uniformly, and only in some domains (e.g., for transport policies, but not energy and food policies). Push-pull packages may also be most acceptable for generic, blanket-type policies that are relatively unpopular (e.g., carbon tax on fuel vehicles). Furthermore, we found that policies that aim to ensure fairness and distributive justice to those on lower incomes can still be perceived as unfair and unjust. Perceptions of fairness also impact beliefs about policy acceptability more generally, and political affiliation impacts how people perceive policies and policy packages. Finally, we find evidence that members of the public may prefer policies which are temporary initially, suggesting that piloting new climate policies and combinations before full implementation may be a productive policy strategy. We further discuss the wider implications and benefits of involving public citizens more directly in the development of policy packages.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional intelligence and humour styles: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Rong Xing; Andrea Williamson; Christopher Williams; Jill Morrison
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Growing evidence has explored how emotional intelligence (EI) and humour
styles interact in shaping adaptive outcomes. However, systematic evidence on this relationship
remains limited. This study aims to systematically review and narratively synthesise the
literature that has investigated the relationship between EI and humour styles.
Methods: A search of five databases – MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, PubMed, and
Psychology and Behavioural Sciences Collection – was performed. Studies were included if
they: (1) were empirical and quantitative; (2) involved adult participants recruited from non-
clinical settings; (3) used variables specifically referred to as humour styles or EI tests; and (4)
were published on or before July 1, 2024.
Results: Of the initial 489 articles identified, nine were included in the qualitative synthesis. EI
was consistently and positively associated with adaptive humour styles (self-enhancing and
affiliative humour) and, in some studies, negatively associated with maladaptive humour styles
(self-defeating and aggressive humour), with small-to-moderate correlations. Trait EI generally
demonstrated closer associations with all humour styles compared to ability EI. Self-enhancing
humour showed the most consistent correlations with both ability and trait EI across all adopted
EI measures. Few and weak correlations were noted concerning aggressive humour.
Conclusions: The present review highlighted the relationship between emotional competencies
and trait humour. A next step in research is to examine ways of fostering appropriate humour
behaviours adapted to specific contexts, and enhancing emotional and social functioning.
Additional effects on low mood, anxiety and social function also could be recorded over time
to identify whether humour enhancement approaches reduce the risks or impact of low mood
or anxiety.

articles_hidden.title: The potential role of memory conversations in children’s suggestibility and in the development of control mechanisms for remembering
articles_hidden.authors: Krisztina Andrási; Alexandra Kelemen; Réka Pető; Zsófia Ginter; Ildikó Király
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory conversations substantially impact the development of children’s autobiographical memory and other capabilities. However, if its impact on memory accuracy is brought into focus, exposure to maternal elaborative conversations may turn out to make children susceptible to suggestions by others; inspiring the question of how these mnemonic practices exactly figure into children’s memory development. We argue that suggestibility might be a consequence of how children are socialized to remember, and thus can be explained by their tendency to rely on the input of other people while recalling their memories. This may result in memory errors when conversation partners have mistaken assumptions about the past. Nevertheless, experience from these mnemonic conversations could also positively impact a number of cognitive abilities – theory of mind, epistemic vigilance or metacognition – which may serve as control processes during retrieval and gradually allow children to discern when to trust their own or other’s testimony about the past, resulting in better memory capabilities in the long run.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Score: Performer Expressivity as a Conduit for Social and Affective Response
articles_hidden.authors: Yenie Lee; Simone Goel; Anna M Palumbo; Pablo Ripolles
articles_hidden.abstract: Music conveys emotion and meaning. Here, we assessed how performers’ expressivity influence listeners’ affective, aesthetic and social-cognitive processes, and how these processes are shaped by individual differences. A total of 275 participants completed an online experiment in either an audiovisual (n = 139) or audio-only (n = 136) condition, in which they viewed or listened to three randomized performances of the same piano work by different world-renowned pianists (Yunchan Lim, Khatia Buniatishvili, and Lang Lang). Following each performance, participants provided affective, aesthetic, and social-cognitive ratings and completed measures of individual differences related to music engagement and social cognition. We found significant Performer (Lim, Buniatishvili, Lang) x Modality (audiovisual, audio-only) interactions for social-cognitive (Connection, Theory of Mind) and specific emotional (Joyful Activation, Sadness) responses, with performer-specific differences being present only in the audiovisual condition. Listener familiarity with the score was the strongest modulator of listener’s experience, whereas empathy, musical reward sensitivity, musical absorption, and Theory of Mind showed selective associations. Our results suggest that musical experience is a multimodal interaction of performer expressivity, sensory modality, and listener characteristics. Furthermore, it supports the idea that visual access to a performance amplifies how listeners construct musical meaning and connection from their interpretation of the performer’s expression and intentions.

articles_hidden.title: AI, Anime, Dolls, and Stories: A Systematic Review into the Role of Fantasy Sexual Materials in Child Sexual Exploitation Escalation Crossover
articles_hidden.authors: Naushaan Ahmad; Sally Kelty; Phillip Sean Kavanagh; Sarah Christofferson
articles_hidden.abstract: This systematic review synthesized evidence from 13 peer-reviewed, empirical studies across a range of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed method designs, to examine the role of fantasy or fictional sexual materials (FSMs) in escalation crossover. Escalation crossover is defined as the transition from non-contact to subsequent contact child sexual offences. A systematic search across EBSCOhost, PubMed, and Scopus and a search of grey literature across Google Scholar and Research Gate was conducted to identify literature relating to FSMs, including child-like sex dolls and virtual child sexual exploitation material (CSEM); including AI-generated CSEM, illustrated CSEM, and text-based CSEM. Findings suggest a bifurcated pattern of FSM engagement, where it can play both a protective/ functional or a risk-enhancing role. Child-like sex doll ownership was suggested as having a protective or functional role; correlated with reductions in compulsive sexual behavior, pornography consumption, and noted as an outlet for individuals in fulfilling their sexual needs. Virtual CSEM was frequently described as a potential gateway of escalation crossover due to the sexualization process being comparable with CSEM, but also as a sexual outlet for non-offending individuals. Multiple studies noted the use of child-like sex dolls and Virtual CSEM concurrently with CSEM engagement. We argue that a balanced, nuanced approach is needed across policy, clinical and legal context. A standardized dictionary of FSMs, and a reconceptualization of escalation crossover is suggested. Implications are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Screen: Self-Reported Accounts of Escalation Crossover in a Darknet Self-identified Pedophile Community
articles_hidden.authors: Naushaan Ahmad; Sarah Christofferson; Sally Kelty; Phillip Sean Kavanagh; Olivia Stanton
articles_hidden.abstract: The proliferation of online communication technologies has fundamentally transformed the landscape of online child sexual exploitation in producing new opportunities for criminal activity and new challenges for risk assessment and prevention. In this study we used an active engagement darknet ethnography approach within a self-identified darknet pedophilia forum to examine respondents’ reported online behaviors, accounts of “crossing the line” from online to contact offending, and self-described profiles and pseudo-moral frameworks. Employing active engagement through structured polls and open-ended questions, data were collected and analyzed quantitatively and qualitatively. Respondents reported a diversity of online behaviors, such as viewing softcore child sexual exploitation material (CSEM), reading fictional CSEM, viewing non-nude content, viewing hardcore CSEM and collecting CSEM, and viewing shotacon or lolicon. Almost half of respondents reported they had “crossed the line”, with the most commonly reported drivers of escalation crossover being opportunity (in combination with disinhibitory factors); engagement with CSEM (notably through desensitization to the content and a desire to produce their own content), together with offense-supportive beliefs internalized through CSEM use; and indulgence in sexual fantasies. Qualitative analysis showed most respondents identified as being “pro-contact pedophiles” (supportive of having sexual relations with children), with a minority identifying as “conservative pedophiles”, implying they were not supportive of sexual relations with children. Our findings, while preliminary, may be indicative of the need for nuanced and individualized approaches to escalation crossover; considering the unique risk profiles of those who transition from online to contact, and how this pathway can be disrupted.

articles_hidden.title: Social camouflaging among autistic adolescents in Japan: Diﬀerential associations with aﬃliate stigma reported by mothers and fathers
articles_hidden.authors: REIRI NAMURA; Siqing Guan; Aya Taniguchi; Sophia Guan; Fumiyo Oshima
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic adolescents’ use of social camouflaging, defined as strategies used to appear less visibly autistic during social interaction, has increasingly been recognized in previous studies; however, its developmental and family context remains unclear. Affiliate stigma, experienced by family members owing to their association with an autistic individual, and internalized stigma, reflecting the incorporation of negative societal beliefs concerning autism into one’s self-concept, may be relevant correlates. Using an online questionnaire survey of 50 autistic adolescent–mother–father triads, this study examined the associations among parental affiliate stigma, autistic adolescents’ internalized stigma, and social camouflaging, while examining maternal and paternal association patterns. Adolescents reported social camouflaging and internalized stigma, and parents reported affiliate stigma. Path analyses, adjusted for age and autistic traits, indicated that autistic adolescents’ internalized stigma was positively associated with social camouflaging. Both maternal and paternal affiliate stigma were positively associated with adolescents’ internalized stigma in the separate maternal and paternal models and remained independently associated with internalized stigma when modeled simultaneously. The estimated indirect association with social camouflaging was only statistically significant for paternal affiliate stigma in the combined model.

articles_hidden.title: Conflict, not category: What the pupil tracks in face pareidolia
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda K Robinson; Jing Liang; Blake William Saurels; Jessica Taubert
articles_hidden.abstract: Illusory faces, the faces people see in inanimate objects, share the low-level image statistics of the objects they are made of while nonetheless being perceived as faces. Neural representations of illusory faces shift from face-like to object-like within roughly 200 ms, and observers explicitly categorise them as objects, yet the illusion remains compelling. We asked whether the pupil, a peripheral index of light and arousal, is sensitive to this dual identity. Forty participants viewed sequences of human faces, illusory faces in objects, and matched non-face objects while performing an orthogonal task at fixation. Human faces and objects both evoked pupil constriction, whereas illusory faces produced dilation beginning at approximately 350 ms. Thus, rather than resembling either category, illusory faces elicited a qualitatively different pupil response. This dissociation remained after controlling for luminance and emotional valence. Critically, within the illusory images the dilation scaled with the strength of the face percept, indexed by independent measures of face categorisation, and did not diminish across repetitions. These findings are consistent with the pupil tracking the conflict between the object and face interpretations, rather than stimulus category per se, revealing a physiological signature of the competing identities that define face pareidolia.

articles_hidden.title: Prospective Gains Introduced During Retrieval Enhance Recognition Sensitivity
articles_hidden.authors: Gizem Filiz; Ian Dobbins
articles_hidden.abstract: Providing incentives encoding reliably enhances subsequent memory, yet their effects at retrieval remain unclear. We contrasted prospective Gains, Losses, and Neutral conditions at retrieval to examine their effects, and we additionally manipulated the nature of feedback provided across three groups (Ntotal = 238). Under Score Change feedback, participants received point increases for accurate responses under Gain trials and point decreases for errors under Loss trials; no other outcomes affected totals. Under Score Change plus Accuracy feedback, participants additionally received trial-by-trial recognition accuracy feedback for all responses, regardless of whether they affected point totals. These groups were contrasted with a No Feedback control group. Across groups, prospective Gains reliably increased recognition sensitivity relative to Neutral prospects by selectively increasing hit rates. Loss prospects produced a mild sensitivity improvement, eliciting a lowered false alarm rate relative to Neutral prospects but only for the Score Change feedback group. Drift diffusion modeling revealed that regardless of feedback group, prospective Gains selectively increased drift rates for old items relative to Neutral and Loss prospects, indicating enhanced recovery of mnemonic evidence. In contrast, prospective Gains and Losses increased boundary separation relative to Neutral trials, reflecting greater response caution. Thus, at retrieval, prospective Gains and Losses have dissociable effects on memory, and the former increase sensitivity providing an adaptive means of prioritizing accurate memory when retrieval yields rewards.

articles_hidden.title: Hierarchical Bayesian models of cardiac interoception in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders with the Heart Rate Discrimination task
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Ryan Kittleson; Claire Hanson; Jesper Fischer Ehmsen; Alisa Zoltowski; Neil Woodward; Carissa Cascio; Micah G. Allen; Julia Sheffield
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Perception of external (exteroceptive) and internal (interoceptive) sensory information is critical for a coherent sense of self, others, and the world. Perception depends on the accuracy and precision of sensory beliefs. Predictive processing models propose that altered sensory beliefs contribute to schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SZ). However, exteroception and interoception are commonly assessed with separate paradigmatic and analysis schemes. We use a Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) paradigm and Bayesian modeling to assess perceptual accuracy and precision during exteroceptive and interoceptive processing in SZ, and test associations with clinical variables. 

Methods 
SZ (N=41) and healthy comparison (HC; N=44) participants completed the HRD and the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness; SZ additionally completed the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale. Hierarchical Bayesian models estimated threshold (bias) and slope (precision), with Bayes factors assessing group difference credibility. 

Results
Participants were less biased and more precise during exteroceptive trials, without evidence of credible group differences in bias. SZ participants had less precise perceptual beliefs overall (BF10=6.74) with no credible group-by-condition interaction. Across all participants, higher interoceptive bias was associated with greater Not-Distracting of internal bodily signals (r=.21, 95% CrI [0.005, 0.41]), and lower interoceptive precision was associated with greater self-reported Body Listening (r=.40, 95% CrI [.08, .67]). Among SZ, lower interoceptive bias was associated with greater positive symptom severity (r=−.29, 95% CrI [−.54, −.01]).

Conclusions 
Sensory beliefs are less precise in SZ. Further, biased interoceptive beliefs relate to psychotic symptoms and subjective bodily awareness. Interventions increasing precision and reducing bias of sensory beliefs may improve psychosis.

articles_hidden.title: Well-Being Visits for Medical Residents: Baseline Assessment of Depression, Anxiety, and Psychological Well-Being in a Graduate Medical Education Program
articles_hidden.authors: Viktoriya Karakcheyeva; Nikhil Derangula; Colleen Roche; Patrick G. Corr
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Physician burnout, depression, anxiety, and psychological distress are significant concerns in graduate medical education (GME). Few programs pair systematic well-being assessments with behavioral health consultations. The George Washington University (GW) Resiliency and Well-being Center (RWC) developed an opt-out well-being visits for incoming residents to establish baseline psychological health and enable early intervention.
Objective
To assess depression, anxiety, and psychological well-being and identify distress patterns not detected through traditional screens.
Methods
Approximately 90 days into residency, 296 residents were invited to complete a survey assessing depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and psychological well-being (WHO-5), followed by a confidential 30-minute well-being visit. Of those invited, 156 (52.7%) responded; 138 (88.5% of respondents) completed at least 1 instrument, and 128 (82.1%) completed all 3. Screening results were analyzed using established thresholds for depression (PHQ-9 ≥10), anxiety (GAD-7 ≥10), and poor psychological well-being (WHO-5 raw score <13).

Minimal symptoms were reported by 70.6% on the PHQ-9 and 70.8% on the GAD-7. Well-being was lower: 26.0% showed poor well-being, 38.2% moderate, and 35.9% good. Profile analysis found that 70.3% had no positive indicators, while 17.2% had poor well-being without clinically significant depression or anxiety. Depression and anxiety correlated strongly (r=0.674). Female residents had higher anxiety scores than male residents (4.17 vs 2.56; P=.018).

Well-being screening identified trainees with diminished psychological well-being despite low levels of clinical depression and anxiety. Findings suggest that well-being may provide information beyond traditional mental health screening. Opt-out well-being visits with validated instruments may facilitate early identification of residents requiring support and inform wellness programming in GME.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Flexible Attention to Magnitude Skill and Executive Function in Math Achievement
articles_hidden.authors: Hyekyung Park; Mary Wagner; Elizabeth Gunderson
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to flexibly switch attention between numerical and spatial magnitudes (FAM skill; e.g., explicitly focusing on size or number, and switching between them when directed) has been theorized as a domain-specific executive function (EF) and found to play an important role in math achievement during early childhood. However, it remains unclear whether FAM skill is related to specific math concepts that support early math learning only, or if it continues to contribute to math achievement through adulthood. We extended previous studies to adulthood by investigating whether FAM skill is distinct from domain-general EF and numerical magnitude processing skill and tested whether FAM skill continues to relate to math achievement beyond childhood. Here, 101 college students completed a FAM task that requires switching attention between magnitude dimensions by comparing either size or number of stars based on a visual cue. We found that in the FAM task, on trials that required switching between magnitudes, adults were less accurate and took longer than trials that did not require switching (i.e., switch cost). More importantly, FAM skill quantified by switch cost error rate predicted math achievement after controlling for domain-general EF, nonsymbolic numerical processing skill, and reading achievement. These results suggest that FAM skill is a distinct cognitive process that is related to math achievement in both childhood and adulthood. Future research can examine the developmental change of this association to better understand through what mechanisms FAM skill continues to contribute to math achievement across the lifespan.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Environmental Structure for Task-general Representation Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Haoxue Fan; Matt R. Nassar
articles_hidden.abstract:
Humans are always facing new tasks, but they are not forced to solve them from scratch, since
they are almost always able to leverage previous experience to scaffold current learning. We
propose that what connects past to present is task-general representations: abstract knowledge of
the structure shared across tasks that serves as a foundation for new learning. Treating tasks
performed in the past as samples from an unknown task distribution, we review how properties
of the observed samples shape task general representations. We apply the same lens to two
different timescales; learning over the course of minutes to days and development over the
course of months to years. We then consider how people exert control over their own task
distributions. We propose that exploration, by diversifying experience, keeps task-general
representations adaptive because people choose their experiences using the very representations
they are learning, errors in those representations can become self-sustaining. Specifically, we
highlight directed and value-free random exploration as two distinct exploration strategies that
correct different distortions in task-general representation.

articles_hidden.title: Tales from the CREP: A Report on Varied Implementations of the Collaborative Replications and Education Project
articles_hidden.authors: Jared Branch; Jordan Rose Wagge; Mark John Brandt; Mona Ibrahim; Alannah Shelby Rivers; Lisa Willoughby; Amanda Mae Woodward; Carole Yue
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: In response to the replication crisis, there is a need for large-scale collaborative replications. Students are well-positioned to contribute to this literature through classroom replications.

Statement of the Problem: Teaching open science practices and engaging students in the replication process is difficult for instructors who have no prior training.

Literature Review: We review literature detailing why instructors choose not to implement replications in the classroom. The Collaborative Replications and Education Project (CREP) provides a template for such efforts, carried out by students under the guidance of an instructor knowledgeable in open science practices. We discuss the outcomes from a series of instructor workshops aimed at teaching instructors of psychology how to implement CREP within classrooms of varying demographics.

Teaching Implications: Five instructors – ranging from private, primarily undergraduate institutes to large, public R1s – discuss their experiences, challenges, and recommendations for including CREP replications in classroom settings.

Conclusion:  The outcomes for students, and lessons learned for instructors, should provide first-time instructors with a guide map for including such efforts within their own classrooms.

articles_hidden.title: Task effects on predictive eye-movements
articles_hidden.authors: Jude Thomas Wells Singleton; Hannah Treadway; Claire Kuntz; Jorge Rodrigo Valdés Kroff; Theres Grüter; Edith Kaan
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on predictive processing has shown that listeners anticipate upcoming linguistic information using linguistic cues, such as verb meaning. Beyond information in the input, listeners’ prediction can also be influenced by top-down control, such as goals and strategies developed in response to a given task. However, it is unclear to what extent evaluations of task relevance modulate top-down control of prediction. We present evidence from two eye-tracking studies in the Visual World Paradigm that associative predictions are largely automatic and not influenced by implicit shifts in the task relevance of a predictive verb. However, when a predictive verb’s task relevance is made explicit in the form of an instruction to predict, prediction is upregulated and initiated earlier irrespective of the verb’s predictiveness, likely due to an enhancement of predictive visual search. Task relevance is thus modulatory for associative prediction when it is specified for listeners.

articles_hidden.title: Framing, Analysis, Interpretation and Two Supplemental Tests for Exploring Serial Mediation Theories with Cross-Sectional Data
articles_hidden.authors: Carl F Weems; Ashley Kuelz; David Sbarra
articles_hidden.abstract: Nonexperimental cross sectional data are frequently used to evaluate mediation and serial mediation hypotheses despite well established limitations for such tests. Associational Variable Analysis (AVA) was introduced to address this problem by reframing mediational language in terms of conditional associations and incremental variance. This paper extends the framing, analysis options, and interpretation guidance in AVA to help researchers improve the analysis and interpretation of studies exploring serial mediation type theories with cross-sectional data. Two supplemental analyses are proposed to aid in the interpretation of such data. One symmetric conditional attenuation, measuring redundancy among the proposed set of variables. The second conditional centrality focused on the proposed mediating variables to examine if they account for a disproportionate share of the conditional dependence relative to the putative independent and dependent variables. Two empirical illustrations are used to demonstrate the framing, set of additional analyses needed to help frame alternative interpretations, and the utility of the two analytic summaries in terms of fostering both the completeness and accuracy of interpretation of such tests and foster incremental science. The first example draws on the data used in the initial AVA paper and the second evaluates a published serial mediation model linking family atmosphere to suicidal ideation through attachment and cognitive flexibility. Code and details for conducting the analyses are provided in supplemental materials. Findings illustrate how the suggested estimates help clarify redundancy, differentiation, and structural organization within multivariable theories thereby providing interpretive guidance for cross sectional analyses where serial mediation conclusions are not defensible.

articles_hidden.title: A thalamocortical mnemonic model of consciousness: thalamic selection of conscious content
articles_hidden.authors: Yimy Amarillo
articles_hidden.abstract: Dominant theories of consciousness (Higher-Order, Global Workspace, Integrated Information and Predictive Processing theories) locate its neural substrate in cortical association areas. I argue that this convergence reflects the technical accessibility of cortical tissue rather than a demonstrated sufficiency of cortical circuits, and I present the Thalamocortical Mnemonic Model of Consciousness (TMMC), which assigns the thalamus a constitutive role in selecting and sustaining conscious content. Content is selected by competition at the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) among thalamic channels, under four selection pressures with identifiable anatomical sources: salience, prediction, value and mnemonic coherence. The mediodorsal nucleus (MD) sustains prefrontal activity once content has arrived, the hippocampus generates episodic endogenous content, the nucleus reuniens coordinates its arrival in prefrontal cortex, and the amygdala biases the competition directly. Building on earlier constructive accounts, the TMMC holds that all conscious content is a configuration of learned cortical patterns; its contribution is the mechanism that selects among them. The model distinguishes two partially dissociable state variables, the level, L(t), and the content, C(t), of consciousness, and three operating modes (exogenous, endogenous and free) whose transitions reflect coupled thalamocortical processes on multiple timescales. Three falsifiable predictions are derived: thalamic precedence over prefrontal cortex for spontaneous thought, accelerated loss of maintained content without delayed generation after MD damage, and thalamus-to-cortex theta-band flow before perceptual switches in binocular rivalry. A further test asks whether the selection pressures dissociate. The TMMC offers a mechanistic alternative to corticocentric models and a research program for thalamocortical consciousness science.

articles_hidden.title: Configural object processing alters intra- and interregional coordination of medial temporal lobe networks
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren Alexandra Homann; Jennifer D. Ryan; Rosanna K. Olsen; Natalia Ladyka-Wojcik; Morgan Barense
articles_hidden.abstract:
Object identity depends on how constituent features are combined, such that the same features
may form distinct objects when their configuration changes. The perirhinal and anterolateral
entorhinal (ERC) cortices are implicated in conjunctive object processing; however, regional
sensitivity alone cannot reveal how information is coordinated across regions, or whether this
coordination extends beyond object-processing regions to spatial and relational regions. Using
generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis of BOLD signals extracted from
manually-segmented medial temporal lobe regions, we examined task-modulated functional
connectivity while younger adults viewed repeated objects (familiar features in familiar
configurations), recombined objects (familiar features in novel configurations), and novel objects
(novel features in novel configurations). This design isolated connectivity changes associated
with configural, featural, and global novelty/familiarity. Configural familiarity (repeated relative
to recombined objects) was associated with widespread increases in connectivity across
distributed hippocampal-cortical networks, encompassing anterior temporal regions implicated in
object processing and posterior-medial and hippocampal regions implicated in relational
processing, including connections with medial prefrontal and posterior-medial cortex. In contrast,
configural novelty (recombined relative to repeated objects) elicited more focal connectivity
increases between right posteromedial ERC and left superior parietal and right frontal regions.
Neither featural novelty/familiarity (recombined vs. novel objects) nor global novelty/familiarity
(repeated vs. novel objects) was associated with significant connectivity differences. We interpret
greater connectivity for configurally familiar repeated objects as reflecting reinstatement of
established conjunctive representations, whereas connectivity changes for configurally novel
recombined objects may reflect the demands of encoding novel conjunctions and/or resolving
competition among partially matching representations.

articles_hidden.title: Are psychedelic users less susceptible to visual illusions? Evidence from the Illusion Game
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski; Marco Sperduti; Oliver Collins; Lucie Daudé; Joy Zogheib; Ewen Kervadec; Bruno Roméo; Pascale Piolino; Baptiste Fauvel
articles_hidden.abstract: Classic psychedelics are thought to relax prior expectations, which should weaken visual illusions. Evidence is scarce, especially outside the acute state, and error rates, the usual measure of illusion sensitivity, also depend on overall performance. We tested 118 adults, of whom 44 had never used a classic psychedelic, 39 had used one within the last 30 days (the "afterglow" period) and 35 longer ago. They completed the Illusion Game, a response-time task of judging which of two targets is larger while the strength of an illusion (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, vertical-horizontal) varies independently of the real difference between them. A hierarchical drift diffusion model was fitted to every choice and response time. Both user groups set wider decision boundaries than naïve participants, gathering more evidence before responding, and made fewer errors. We then computed an index of illusion sensitivity independent of overall accuracy: the effect of illusion strength on performance relative to that of the real difference. This index was 22% lower in users on average, equally in recent and past users, and unrelated to age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the intensity of the last experience. It correlated moderately across illusions, less than general performance did. Psychedelic users appeared somewhat less sensitive to illusions, as relaxed priors would predict, but the absence of a clear link with use recency limits interpretative confidence and generalizability.

articles_hidden.title: Interoceptive Disruptions and Childhood Trauma: Validation of the Polish version of the Scale of Body Connection
articles_hidden.authors: martyna bachar; Julia Chmielewska; Magdalena Berent; Aleksandra Maria Herman; Małgorzata Dragan
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study aimed to evaluate the structure of the Polish version of the Scale of Body
Connection (SBC) and whether bodily dissociation mediates the link between adverse
childhood experiences (ACEs) and alexithymia. An online sample (N = 271, M = 23.49
years) completed the 10-item ACE scale, the Perth Alexithymia Questionnaire Short
Form (PAQ-S), and the SBC. A total of 209 participants (77.12%) reported having
experienced at least one ACE in their childhood, and as many as 57 (21.03%) reported
at least four ACEs. Regarding SBC, results showed Cronbach’s alpha coefficients of
.84 for Body Awareness (BA) and .77 for bodily dissociation (BD). Confirmatory factor
analysis (CFA) showed inadequate fit for the original two-factor model (robust CFI =
.71). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) supported a four-factor structure, where
following factors have been distinguished: BA1 (Body Awareness), BA2 (Noticing
Negative States), BD1 (Difficulties in Processing Emotions), and BD2 (Detachment
from the Body). Because BD1 demonstrated insufficient discriminant validity from
alexithymia, only BD2 was retained as a mediator. The mediation analysis revealed a
significant indirect association between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and
alexithymia through bodily detachment (β = .07, 95% CI [.02, .13], p = .008). ACE
exposure explained 3.0% of the variance in bodily detachment (R² = .030), while ACE
exposure and bodily detachment together explained 16.6% of the variance in
alexithymia (R² = .17). These findings provide preliminary support for a four-factor
structure of the SBC in a Polish sample and suggest that bodily detachment may play
an important role in the association between childhood adversity and difficulties in
emotional awareness and processing. Future research should examine the stability
and replicability of the proposed factor structure, investigate the indirect association in
independent samples, and identify additional factors contributing to bodily detachment
and alexithymia.

articles_hidden.title: lmmresample: Resampling inference for mixed models of pupillometry and other trial-structured physiological signals. A tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Ricardo Martínez Flores; Hams Super
articles_hidden.abstract: Continuous physiological signals such as pupil size, EEG, skin conductance and heart rate are often analysed with linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) of the complete time series. Because consecutive samples are strongly autocorrelated, the usual Wald and Satterthwaite tests treat them as nearly independent and overstate the evidence. We present lmmresample, an R package that keeps the researcher's LMM and replaces its inference with permutation tests and bootstrap confidence intervals that resample whole trials and participants, so that the dependence within trials is carried into the reference distribution without being modelled. The package also corrects for multiple tests and post hoc comparisons, and includes diagnostics that check the model fit, quantify the dependence and calibrate the tests for the user's design. In simulations resembling pupillometry data, Wald and Satterthwaite tests of condition × time interactions gave 46–83% false positives, and their 95% intervals covered the true value in 57–68% of data sets. The permutation test held the nominal level (2–7%) in every scenario, and bootstrap intervals covered 91–96%. A tutorial with public pupillometry data shows a complete workflow, including an analysis in which Wald, Satterthwaite and GAMM tests indicated an effect that methods controlling the error rate did not support. For continuous signals analysed with mixed models, lmmresample gives p-values and confidence intervals that keep their nominal error rate and coverage. The dependence between samples does not have to be specified, no complex random-effects structure has to be fitted, and power matched the best valid alternative.

articles_hidden.title: The Intellectual Justice Scale: Measuring How Fairly People Engage With Knowledge
articles_hidden.authors: Yara Daamen; Vlasta Sikimić; Daniel Lakens
articles_hidden.abstract: Intellectual justice, the disposition to engage fairly with knowledge and those who produce it, has received growing attention in philosophy and education, yet no validated self-report measure exists. We developed and validated the Intellectual Justice Scale (IJS), a 9-item measure with three factors (Testimonial Justice, Hermeneutical Justice, and Intellectual Action) grounded in Fricker’s framework of intellectual injustice. An initial item pool was refined through expert review and pilot testing. In Study 1 (N = 404), exploratory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure, with independent statistical and conceptual item selection converging on the same nine items. In Study 2 (N = 401), confirmatory factor analysis supported good model fit, and the IJS showed expected associations with intellectual humility, personality traits, and social justice attitudes while remaining empirically distinguishable from each. These findings offer the first validated self-report measure of intellectual justice attitudes, providing researchers with a tool to study individual differences.

articles_hidden.title: Impossibility and Logical Contradictions Can Enhance the Perceived Value of Fictional Theological Propositions
articles_hidden.authors: Takuetsu Yajima; Minh-Thi Nguyen; Eisuke Niida; Yo Nakawake
articles_hidden.abstract: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities. It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people’s evaluations of religious propositions. In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability. Those propositions were rated for impossibility and logical contradiction. A composite positive-evaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The result shows higher impossibility and higher logical contradiction predict higher positive evaluations of the propositions. These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of meal irregularity and uncertainty on health: piloting a protocol to manipulate key features of food insecurity in food-secure women
articles_hidden.authors: Melissa Bateson; Eleanor Hayes; Adrian Holliday; Courtney Neal; Wouter Peeters; Oliver Shannon
articles_hidden.abstract: Food insecurity (FI) is associated with obesity and poor physical and mental health, but whether it causes these outcomes is unknown. In a mixed 2 × 2 cross-over design, participants completed two 2-week interventions with regular or irregular meal schedules and were either informed of or uncertain about their schedule in advance. Dietary recalls confirmed that the irregularity manipulation altered eating patterns, and post-intervention questionnaires confirmed that the uncertainty manipulation increased worry about meal timing. In Part B, we compared outcomes before and after each intervention. None of our preregistered predictions was supported: irregular meals did not reduce diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT), uncertainty did not amplify any effect of irregularity and uncertainty did not increase anxiety or depression symptoms. However, equivalence tests could not exclude meaningful effects. Exploratory analyses, including a pooled analysis of the three preregistered outcomes, suggested that, rather than uncertainty amplifying the effects of irregularity, any departure from a regular meal schedule known in advance may be sufficient to shift health-relevant outcomes including DIT, food intake and affective state. With modifications, this protocol could be used in adequately powered trials to test whether meal irregularity and uncertainty contribute to the health effects of FI.

articles_hidden.title: Examining HiTOP Through Naturalistic Symptom Descriptions in Anonymous Online Mental Health Forums: A Mixed-Methods Study Protocol
articles_hidden.authors: Drin Ferizaj
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) organises covarying symptoms and maladaptive traits into transdiagnostic dimensions to address limitations of categorical diagnosis. Naturalistic symptom descriptions may complement structured assessments. Objective: This protocol describes a reproducible mixed-methods workflow to derive symptom indicators from forum posts and examine their organisation relative to HiTOP. Methods and analysis: The target sample is 80,000 public Reddit posts. After local de-identification, a large language model (LLM) will extract symptom labels and supporting paraphrases. Two human experts will independently review outputs for up to 250 posts. Three embedding models will flag potentially equivalent symptom labels for local LLM assessment. Two experts will qualitatively review the most frequent canonical symptom labels (at least 1,000) and develop a codebook of symptom categories, continuing until a prespecified saturation criterion is met. An LLM will assign canonical symptom labels to these categories, producing binary post-level indicators. Multiverse-inspired structural analyses will compare network, component, factor, and clustering representations across discovery, internal tuning, and holdout partitions. Evaluation will assess interpretability, stability, and agreement with expert mapping to HiTOP. Supplementary analyses will include agent-assisted exploration, codebook application to DepressionEmo and the Reddit Mental Health Dataset, and pooled integrative analysis that may include additional comparable corpora.
Discussion: The study will examine whether symptom co-expression within posts forms interpretable patterns corresponding to HiTOP.
Ethics: The Ethics Committee of Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin approved the study (EA2/274/25). The study was preregistered on 8 May 2026 (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00040244).

articles_hidden.title: Remembering the unfolding of emotional events: Reduced temporal compression for negative but not positive events
articles_hidden.authors: Charline Colson; Arnaud D'Argembeau
articles_hidden.abstract: The time required to remember an event is typically shorter than the actual duration of the past episode. Recent research has shown that this temporal compression is less pronounced for negative than for neutral events, suggesting enhanced preservation of event unfolding. The present study examined whether this effect extends to positive events. Participants watched positive, negative, and neutral videos and then mentally replayed them before verbally describing and subjectively evaluating their memories. Replicating previous findings, negative events were replayed with less temporal compression than neutral events and were described with longer and more episodically detailed narratives. In contrast, positive events did not differ from neutral events on any of these objective measures, although both negative and positive memories were rated as more detailed, more dynamic, and less difficult to recall than neutral ones. These findings suggest a valence asymmetry in the representation of event unfolding: negative emotion preserves more of an event’s temporal course, whereas positive emotion enhances the subjective experience of remembering without enriching the objective representation of how the event unfolded.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Stressors: The Role of Personal Vulnerability in Subjective Mental Well-Being in Farming Communities in the United Kingdom and Canada
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Nyczaj Kyle; Emma Barkus; Andria Jones; Stephen Dunne
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Farmers, their families, and employees face daily stressors that can adversely affect their mental well-being. To better understand stress and mental well-being in farming populations, this study examines this relationship in the United Kingdom (UK) and Canada. 
Method: Using an online cross-sectional survey, 569 adults from farming communities (37% male, 63% female; Mage = 47.57, SD = 12.55) completed measures of stress event load (EL), personal vulnerability to stress (PV), and subjective mental well-being. Data were analysed using hierarchical multiple regression, with simple-slopes analysis, and analysis of variance. 
Results: Higher PV was associated with lower mental well-being, after accounting for EL (unstandardised B = -.40, 95% CI [-.45, -.35]). Although a significant interaction between EL and PV was observed (unstandardised B = .02, 95% CI [.01, .02]), after Bonferroni correction, higher EL was significantly associated with higher mental well-being only among participants with high PV. ANOVA also identified significant differences between stress-risk groups (ηp² = .31), with participants in high PV groups reporting the lowest well-being. 
Conclusion: While studies have traditionally focused on farming-specific sources of stress, this research suggests that understanding mental well-being in farming communities requires considering not only the volume of stressors people face but also their perceived capacity to cope. Future research should examine individual coping capacities alongside the economic and structural sources of stress using longitudinal measures to clarify the associations between psychological resources, stress, and mental well-being.

articles_hidden.title: The Supporting Role of Women in UK Farming. A Mixed Methods Analysis of Relational Need Satisfaction, Stress, and Well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Nyczaj Kyle; Stephen Dunne; Andria Jones; Emma Barkus
articles_hidden.abstract:
Healthy relationships are essential for well-being and can buffer against stress. Women in the farming community may face challenges that compromise maintaining supportive relationships. We provide novel data investigating satisfaction of relationship needs for women in farming. 
138 women (Mage = 48.46 years, SD = 12.31) from the UK farming community completed online mixed-methods questionnaire comprising qualitative and quantitative measures of well-being, stress, relational need satisfaction, and reciprocity. 
Met relational needs were associated with higher well-being and lower stress. Moderation analysis showed higher stress was linked to lower well-being at fulfilled relational needs. This striking result was supported by qualitative data: while women provide support to others, they receive limited support in return.
The complex dynamics of reciprocal social support among women in farming suggest the agricultural lifestyle can both promote and obstruct relational need satisfaction. Replicating the findings is important to explore differences in relationships across farming roles.

articles_hidden.title: Let’s protect us Europeans from them: Emotional predictors of outgroup solidarity, ingroup defense, and outgroup derogation in response to the Ukrainian war (2022 – 2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Janine Stollberg; Julius Möller; Stefan Reiss; Eva Jonas
articles_hidden.abstract: The Russian invasion of Ukraine has threatened Europe’s safety and economy. Europeans responded with solidarity towards Ukrainians, demonstrated ingroup strength, but also expressed derogatory attitudes towards Russians and mistrusted public media. Interestingly, feelings of being moved were negatively associated with outgroup derogation and media mistrust, supporting being moved as a collective approach emotion binding Europeans together while reducing negative consequences. articles_hidden.title: Not All Fakes Are Equally Ugly: The Anti-AI Bias in Aesthetic Judgment and the Role of Affect, Self-Relevance, and Authenticity
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski; Ana Neves; Giulia Cabbai; Guido Corradi; Marco VIOLA; Marco Sperduti
articles_hidden.abstract: Art is devalued once it is attributed to artificial intelligence (AI). Whether this anti-AI bias is a generic penalty for non-original works or specific to the absence of a human author is unknown, as is how long it lasts. In a preregistered study, 324 participants rated 48 genuine human paintings, each presented as an Original, a human Forgery or AI-Generated, on beauty, valence, meaningfulness and monetary worth, then judged how synthetic (AI vs. human) and authentic (copy vs. original) each was. Forgeries were rated below Originals on every dimension, and AI-Generated works about twice as low, the AI-specific penalty falling most heavily on meaningfulness. The labels did not alter gaze, and their effects did not depend on the emotional content or personal relevance of the artworks. Artworks labelled AI-Generated were judged more synthetic and, less clearly, Forgeries less original, and the more beautiful an artwork, the more likely it was judged human-made, even when unlabelled. About six weeks later (n = 220), after learning that all artworks were human originals, participants no longer rated previously AI-labelled works as less beautiful. They had forgotten the labels but remembered what they had believed, and reconstructed the labels from these beliefs and their initial appraisal. The bias tracked attitudes toward AI, not interoceptive sensibility or visual imagery. The anti-AI bias thus combines a generic non-originality penalty with a penalty specific to the missing human author: it acts at the moment of judgment, yet leaves beliefs that outlast the memory of the label.

articles_hidden.title: Free-text responses improve prediction of mental health outcomes after psychedelic experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Fritz Guenther; Mathis Parent-Couture; Abdo Uyar; Klara Wieczorke; Ulrike Lueken; Ricarda Evens; Max Wolff

Mental health surveys and studies regularly ask participants to describe their experiences in their own words. analyses. In three datasets on psychedelic experiences (229–958 participants), we tested whether text embeddings of participants’ free-text responses improve held-out predictions of five mental health outcomes beyond 20–45 demographic, setting, and questionnaire
